sources.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)
sources.authority: Primary paper introducing Raft, the consensus algorithm underlying etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, and most modern replicated logs.

facts.claim: Raft separates leader election, log replication, and safety as independent subproblems
facts.quote: Raft decomposes the consensus problem into three relatively independent subproblems... Leader election... Log replication... Safety

facts.claim: A 43-student user study found Raft significantly easier to understand than Paxos
facts.quote: A user study with 43 students at two universities shows that Raft is significantly easier to understand than Paxos: after learning both algorithms, 33 of these students were able to answer questions about Raft better than questions about Paxos.

facts.claim: A cluster of 5 servers tolerates the failure of any 2
facts.quote: a typical cluster of five servers can tolerate the failure of any two servers

facts.claim: Election timeouts are randomized from a fixed interval, e.g. 150-300ms, to avoid repeated split votes
facts.quote: election timeouts are chosen randomly from a fixed interval (e.g., 150-300ms)

facts.claim: A log entry is committed once a majority of the cluster has replicated it; a minority of slow servers does not affect performance
facts.quote: a command can complete as soon as a majority of the cluster has responded to a single round of remote procedure calls; a minority of slow servers need not impact overall system performance

facts.claim: Raft uses a strong leader: log entries flow only from leader to followers, simplifying management
facts.quote: Strong leader: Raft uses a stronger form of leadership than other consensus algorithms. For example, log entries only flow from the leader to other servers.

facts.claim: Raft's membership-change mechanism uses joint consensus with overlapping majorities of old and new configurations so the cluster keeps operating during reconfiguration
facts.quote: Raft's mechanism for changing the set of servers in the cluster uses a new joint consensus approach where the majorities of two different configurations overlap during transitions

sources.title: The Google File System
sources.authors: Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff, Shun-Tak Leung
sources.authority: Primary paper on GFS, the distributed file system underlying Bigtable and the architectural template for HDFS.

facts.claim: GFS clusters store hundreds of terabytes across thousands of disks on over a thousand machines, accessed concurrently by hundreds of clients
facts.quote: The largest cluster to date provides hundreds of terabytes of storage across thousands of disks on over a thousand machines, and it is concurrently accessed by hundreds of clients.

facts.claim: Chunk size is 64 MB, much larger than typical filesystem block sizes
facts.quote: Chunk size is one of the key design parameters... We have chosen 64 MB, which is much larger than typical file system block sizes.

facts.claim: GFS uses a single master architecture; clients never read/write file data through the master, only metadata
facts.quote: Having a single master vastly simplifies our design... Clients never read and write file data through the master.

facts.claim: Each chunk is replicated on multiple chunkservers (default 3 replicas), with configurable replication levels per namespace region
facts.quote: For reliability, each chunk is replicated on multiple chunkservers. By default, we store three replicas, though users can designate different replication levels for different regions of the file namespace.

facts.claim: The master maintains less than 64 bytes of metadata per 64MB chunk, keeping the entire metadata working set in memory
facts.quote: The master maintains less than 64 bytes of metadata for each 64 MB chunk.

facts.claim: Atomic record append lets many clients append concurrently without extra client-side synchronization, at an offset chosen by GFS
facts.quote: GFS provides an atomic append operation called record append... the client specifies only the data. GFS appends it to the file at least once atomically... and returns that offset to the client.

facts.claim: Mutation order is controlled via leases: the master grants a chunk lease to one replica (the primary) with a 60-second initial timeout, renewable via piggybacked HeartBeat messages
facts.quote: The lease mechanism is designed to minimize management overhead at the master. A lease has an initial timeout of 60 seconds.

facts.claim: Ideal elapsed time to push B bytes to R replicas is B/T + RL, with typical network throughput T of 100 Mbps and latency L well under 1ms, so 1MB distributes in about 80ms
facts.quote: the ideal elapsed time for transferring B bytes to R replicas is B/T + RL where T is the network throughput... Our network links are typically 100 Mbps (T) and L is far below 1 ms. Therefore, 1 MB can ideally be distributed in about 80 ms.

sources.title: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data
sources.authors: Fay Chang, Jeffrey Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, Wilson C. Hsieh, Deborah A. Wallach, Mike Burrows, Tushar Chandra, Andrew Fikes, Robert E. Gruber
sources.authority: Primary paper on Bigtable, Google's wide-column store underlying web indexing, Google Earth, Google Finance, and part of the Spanner storage stack.

facts.claim: Bigtable's data model is a sparse, distributed, persistent multi-dimensional sorted map indexed by (row, column, timestamp)
facts.quote: (row:string, column:string, time:int64) -> string

facts.claim: Row ranges are dynamically partitioned into tablets, the unit of distribution and load balancing; tables start as one tablet and split automatically to ~100-200MB by default
facts.quote: Bigtable maintains data in lexicographic order by row key. The row range for a table is dynamically partitioned. Each row range is called a tablet

facts.claim: Bigtable uses the Chubby lock service (Paxos-based, five replicas) to ensure at most one active master and to store bootstrap/schema/ACL data
facts.quote: Bigtable relies on a highly-available and persistent distributed lock service called Chubby... A Chubby service consists of five active replicas, one of which is elected to be the master

facts.claim: Data is stored on GFS using the immutable SSTable file format with a 64KB block size and an in-memory block index
facts.quote: An SSTable provides a persistent, ordered immutable map from keys to values... each block is 64KB in size

facts.claim: A tablet server typically manages 10 to a thousand tablets
facts.quote: Each tablet server manages a set of tablets (typically we have somewhere between ten to a thousand tablets per tablet server)

facts.claim: Measured Chubby unavailability affected Bigtable server-hours by only 0.0047% on average across 14 clusters/11 Chubby instances (worst single cluster: 0.0326%)
facts.quote: The average percentage of Bigtable server hours during which some data stored in Bigtable was not available due to Chubby unavailability... was 0.0047%. The percentage for the single cluster that was most affected by Chubby unavailability was 0.0326%.

facts.claim: Bigtable does not support general cross-row transactions, only single-row atomic read-modify-write
facts.quote: Bigtable supports several other features... Bigtable supports single-row transactions... Bigtable does not currently support general transactions across row keys.

sources.title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
sources.authors: James C. Corbett, Jeffrey Dean, Michael Epstein, et al.
sources.authority: Primary paper on Spanner, the first system to provide externally-consistent distributed transactions at global scale via the TrueTime API; the architectural successor to Bigtable/Megastore at Google.

facts.claim: Spanner shards data across many sets of Paxos state machines in datacenters spread all over the world
facts.quote: it is a database that shards data across many sets of Paxos [21] state machines in datacenters spread all over the world

facts.claim: At least 300 applications within Google use Megastore, including Gmail, Picasa, Calendar, Android Market, and AppEngine, despite its relatively low performance, because its data model is simpler to manage
facts.quote: At least 300 applications within Google use Megastore (despite its relatively low performance) because its data model is simpler to manage... Examples of well-known Google applications that use Megastore are Gmail, Picasa, Calendar, Android Market, and AppEngine.

facts.claim: A zone has one zonemaster and between one hundred and several thousand spanservers; each spanserver is responsible for 100 to 1000 tablets
facts.quote: A zone has one zonemaster and between one hundred and several thousand spanservers... each spanserver is responsible for between 100 and 1000 instances of a data structure called a tablet

facts.claim: Each spanserver implements a single Paxos state machine on top of each tablet, with long-lived leases defaulting to 10 seconds; every Paxos write is logged twice (tablet log and Paxos log)
facts.quote: Our Paxos implementation supports long-lived leaders with time-based leader leases, whose length defaults to 10 seconds... the current Spanner implementation logs every Paxos write twice: once in the tablet's log, and once in the Paxos log.

facts.claim: A directory (bucket of contiguous keys sharing a prefix) is the unit of data placement and geographic replication; a 50MB directory can typically be moved between Paxos groups in a few seconds
facts.quote: A directory is also the smallest unit whose geographic-replication properties... can be specified by an application... One could expect that a 50MB directory can be moved in a few seconds.

facts.claim: Spanner exposes a novel TrueTime API that directly exposes clock uncertainty, keeping it generally under 10ms using GPS and atomic clock references
facts.quote: The API directly exposes clock uncertainty... This implementation keeps uncertainty small (generally less than 10ms) by using multiple modern clock references (GPS and atomic clocks).

facts.claim: Spanner is the first system to provide externally-consistent distributed transactions at global scale, with commit timestamps reflecting serialization order
facts.quote: Spanner is the first system to distribute data at global scale and support externally-consistent distributed transactions.

conflicts: Bigtable (S3) provides only eventually-consistent replication across datacenters and no cross-row transactions; Spanner (S4) explicitly built synchronous cross-datacenter replication and general-purpose transactions to fix this, at the cost of running two-phase commit over Paxos.

sources.title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store
sources.authors: Giuseppe DeCandia, Deniz Hastorun, Madan Jampani, et al.
sources.authority: Primary paper on Dynamo, the eventually-consistent key-value store whose design (consistent hashing, vector clocks, quorum reads/writes, gossip) became the blueprint for Cassandra, Riak, Voldemort, and DynamoDB.

facts.claim: Dynamo deliberately sacrifices consistency under certain failure scenarios to achieve high availability, using an 'always writeable' design that never rejects customer updates
facts.quote: To achieve this level of availability, Dynamo sacrifices consistency under certain failure scenarios... Dynamo targets the design space of an 'always writeable' data store (i.e., a data store that is highly available for writes).

facts.claim: SLAs at Amazon are expressed at the 99.9th percentile, not the mean or median, because averages don't reflect the experience of the whole customer base
facts.quote: At Amazon, SLAs are expressed and measured at the 99.9th percentile of the distribution... These metrics are not good enough if the goal is to build a system where all customers have a good experience.

facts.claim: Data is partitioned and replicated using consistent hashing with virtual nodes; conflicting writes are reconciled via vector clocks
facts.quote: Dynamo uses a synthesis of well known techniques to achieve scalability and availability: Data is partitioned and replicated using consistent hashing, and consistency is facilitated by object versioning.

facts.claim: Consistency among replicas during updates is maintained by a quorum-like technique and a decentralized replica synchronization protocol using Merkle trees for anti-entropy
facts.quote: Recovering from permanent failures: Anti-entropy using Merkle trees; Synchronizes divergent replicas in the background.

facts.claim: Initial Dynamo instances target a scale of up to hundreds of storage hosts
facts.quote: its initial design targets a scale of up to hundreds of storage hosts

facts.claim: Membership and failure detection use a gossip-based protocol, avoiding a centralized registry
facts.quote: Membership and failure detection: Gossip-based membership protocol and failure detection. Preserves symmetry and avoids having a centralized registry for storing membership and node liveness information.

facts.claim: Dynamo compares itself explicitly to Bigtable: Dynamo targets pure key/value access requiring high write availability where updates are never rejected, even during partitions
facts.quote: Compared to Bigtable, Dynamo targets applications that require only key/value access with primary focus on high availability where updates are not rejected even in the wake of network partitions or server failures.

conflicts: Dynamo (S5) explicitly rejects the relational/ACID model used by Spanner (S4) for the same class of always-on shopping-cart-like services, arguing 'experience at Amazon has shown that data stores that provide ACID guarantees tend to have poor availability.'

sources.title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters
sources.authority: Primary paper defining the MapReduce programming model and runtime, the ancestor of Hadoop and the batch-processing lineage that Spark and Flink respond to.

facts.claim: The map function has type (k1,v1) -> list(k2,v2); reduce has type (k2,list(v2)) -> list(v2)
facts.quote: map (k1,v1) -> list(k2,v2); reduce (k2,list(v2)) -> list(v2)

facts.claim: Input is split into M pieces of 16-64MB (user-controllable); the master assigns idle workers to map or reduce tasks
facts.quote: the MapReduce library... splits the input files into M pieces of typically 16 megabytes to 64 megabytes (MB) per piece

facts.claim: On worker failure, completed and in-progress map tasks are reset to idle and rescheduled because their output is on local disk (inaccessible); completed reduce tasks need not be redone since output is in the global file system
facts.quote: Completed map tasks are re-executed on a failure because their output is stored on the local disk(s) of the failed machine... Completed reduce tasks do not need to be re-executed since their output is stored in a global file system.

facts.claim: Hundreds of MapReduce programs have been implemented and upwards of one thousand MapReduce jobs run on Google's clusters every day
facts.quote: hundreds of MapReduce programs have been implemented and upwards of one thousand MapReduce jobs are executed on Google's clusters every day

facts.claim: Typical clusters consist of hundreds/thousands of dual-processor x86 machines with 2-4GB RAM, connected by 100Mbps-1Gbps Ethernet, with commodity IDE disks
facts.quote: Machines are typically dual-processor x86 processors running Linux, with 2-4 GB of memory per machine... typically either 100 megabits/second or 1 gigabit/second at the machine level

sources.title: Zanzibar: Google's Consistent, Global Authorization System
sources.authors: Ruoming Pang, Ramon Caceres, Mike Burrows, et al.
sources.authority: Primary paper on Zanzibar, Google's global relationship-based authorization system used by Calendar, Cloud, Drive, Maps, Photos, and YouTube; the model behind the open-source SpiceDB/OpenFGA authz systems.

facts.claim: Zanzibar stores more than two trillion access control lists and performs millions of authorization checks per second
facts.quote: Zanzibar operates at a global scale along multiple dimensions. It stores more than two trillion ACLs and performs millions of authorization checks per second.

facts.claim: Zanzibar has maintained 95th-percentile latency under 10ms and availability above 99.999% over 3 years of production use
facts.quote: It has maintained 95th-percentile latency of less than 10 milliseconds and availability of greater than 99.999% over 3 years of production use.

facts.claim: ACLs are relation tuples of the form <object>#<relation>@<user>, and can be group tuples where the user is itself a userset, supporting nested group membership
facts.quote: <tuple> ::= <object>'#'<relation>'@'<user>... One feature worth noting is that a userset allows a client to refer to groups and thus supports representing nested group membership.

facts.claim: Zanzibar provides external consistency for authorization decisions via a globally distributed database with 'zookies', letting a client ensure a check reflects ACL data no older than a specified change
facts.quote: Zanzibar provides these ordering properties by storing ACLs in a globally distributed database system with external consistency guarantees.

facts.claim: Zanzibar responds to more than 95% of authorization checks within 10 milliseconds and has maintained more than 99.999% availability for the last 3 years
facts.quote: Zanzibar responds to more than 95% of authorization checks within 10 milliseconds and has maintained more than 99.999% availability for the last 3 years.

sources.title: ZooKeeper: Wait-free Coordination for Internet-scale Systems
sources.authors: Patrick Hunt, Mahadev Konar, Flavio P. Junqueira, Benjamin Reed
sources.authority: Primary paper on ZooKeeper, the coordination kernel behind leader election, service discovery, and distributed locks in Kafka, HBase, and countless other systems; the direct ancestor to etcd's design goals.

facts.claim: ZooKeeper guarantees FIFO client ordering of all operations and linearizable writes, but reads are served locally by any server and are not linearized, since read workloads dominate at ratios of 2:1 to 100:1
facts.quote: We show for the target workloads, 2:1 to 100:1 read to write ratio, that ZooKeeper can handle tens to hundreds of thousands of transactions per second.

facts.claim: ZooKeeper implements a leader-based atomic broadcast protocol called Zab to guarantee update linearizability
facts.quote: To guarantee that update operations satisfy linearizability, we implement a leader-based atomic broadcast protocol [23], called Zab [24].

facts.claim: Data is organized as znodes in a hierarchical namespace like a filesystem; znodes are typed regular or ephemeral (deleted when the creating session ends)
facts.quote: There are two types of znodes that a client can create: Regular... Ephemeral: Clients create such znodes, and they either delete them explicitly, or let the system remove them automatically when the session that creates them terminates

facts.claim: Watches let clients receive one-time notifications of znode changes without polling; this is the primitive used to build leader election and locks on top
facts.quote: ZooKeeper implements watches to allow clients to receive timely notifications of changes without requiring polling.

facts.claim: ZooKeeper is described as a wait-free coordination kernel deliberately exposing simple primitives (not blocking locks) so applications can build their own higher-level coordination recipes
facts.quote: Since ZooKeeper is part of critical infrastructure, ZooKeeper aims to provide a simple and high performance kernel for building more complex coordination primitives at the client.

sources.title: Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg
sources.authors: Abhishek Verma, Luis Pedrosa, Madhukar Korupolu, David Oppenheimer, Eric Tune, John Wilkes
sources.authority: Primary paper on Borg, Google's cluster manager and the direct design ancestor of Kubernetes; grounds cluster scheduling, admission control, and priority/quota mechanisms used across both classical services and AI training clusters.

facts.claim: Borg cells run up to tens of thousands of machines; median cell size is about 10K machines
facts.quote: Borg cells run hundreds of thousands of jobs, from many thousands of different applications, across a number of clusters each with up to tens of thousands of machines... Our median cell size is about 10k machines

facts.claim: Borg's workload has two main parts: long-running latency-sensitive services (e.g. Gmail, Docs, web search, BigTable) and batch jobs taking seconds to days
facts.quote: Such services are used for end-user-facing products such as Gmail, Google Docs, and web search, and for internal infrastructure services (e.g., BigTable). The second is batch jobs that take from a few seconds to a few days to complete.

facts.claim: In a representative cell, prod jobs get ~70% of CPU resources allocated and ~60% of CPU usage; ~55% of memory allocated and ~85% of memory usage
facts.quote: prod jobs are allocated about 70% of the total CPU resources and represent about 60% of the total CPU usage; they are allocated about 55% of the total memory and represent about 85% of the total memory usage

facts.claim: Admission control uses priority and quota: quota is checked at admission time (not scheduling time) and jobs with insufficient quota are rejected immediately upon submission
facts.quote: Quota-checking is part of admission control, not scheduling: jobs with insufficient quota are immediately rejected upon submission.

facts.claim: Every task gets a stable 'Borg name service' (BNS) name recorded in Chubby that load balancers use to find where to route requests
facts.quote: Borg creates a stable 'Borg name service' (BNS) name for each task that includes the cell name, job name, and task number. Borg writes the task's hostname and port into a consistent, highly-available file in Chubby with this name

facts.claim: A preempted task typically gets a SIGTERM notice about 80% of the time before SIGKILL
facts.quote: The actual notice may be less if the preemptor sets a delay bound. In practice, a notice is delivered about 80% of the time.

sources.title: Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing
sources.authors: Jay Kreps, Neha Narkhede, Jun Rao
sources.authority: Primary paper by Kafka's creators, describing the design decisions (log-structured storage, pull model, stateless broker) that define the messaging/streaming lineage used across Part A and referenced across AI training data pipelines.

facts.claim: Each topic partition corresponds to a physical log implemented as a set of ~1GB segment files; a message is only exposed to consumers after being flushed
facts.quote: Physically, a log is implemented as a set of segment files of approximately the same size (e.g., 1GB)... A message is only exposed to the consumers after it is flushed.

facts.claim: Kafka relies on the OS page cache instead of an application-level cache, so a restarted broker keeps a warm cache
facts.quote: we rely on the underlying file system page cache. This has the main benefit of avoiding double buffering... This has the additional benefit of retaining warm cache even when a broker process is restarted.

facts.claim: Kafka uses a pull model (consumers pull from brokers) rather than push, which allows a consumer to deliberately rewind and re-consume data, unlike a queue
facts.quote: At LinkedIn we find the 'pull' model more suitable for our applications... A consumer can deliberately rewind back to an old offset and re-consume data. This violates the common contract of a queue, but proves to be an essential feature.

facts.claim: The broker is stateless: it does not track which messages each consumer has read; a message is deleted after a fixed retention period, typically 7 days
facts.quote: Unlike most other messaging systems, in Kafka, the information about how much each consumer has consumed is not maintained by the broker, but by the consumer itself... typically 7 days.

facts.claim: Messages are addressed by logical offset in the log rather than an explicit message id, avoiding auxiliary index structures
facts.quote: a message stored in Kafka doesn't have an explicit message id. Instead, each message is addressed by its logical offset in the log.

facts.claim: Kafka uses sendfile() to transfer bytes from a log segment file to a socket without extra copies or kernel-user boundary crossings for efficient transfer
facts.quote: Kafka exploits the sendfile API [5] that can directly transfer bytes from a file channel to a socket channel. This typically avoids 2 of the copies and 1 system call.

sources.title: Problems with CAP, and Yahoo's little known NoSQL system
sources.org: DBMS Musings (personal blog; author later at Yale/UMD)
sources.version: Published 2010-04-23; formalized as PACELC in Computer, Feb 2012
sources.authority: Primary source (original post) for the PACELC framework, which is the formulation Aman's learner profile and content standards expect over a bare CAP theorem treatment.

facts.claim: PACELC asks: if there is a partition (P), how does the system trade off availability and consistency (A and C); else (E), in normal operation, how does it trade off latency and consistency (L and C)?
facts.quote: if there is a partition (P) how does the system tradeoff between availability and consistency (A and C); else (E) when the system is running as normal in the absence of partitions, how does the system tradeoff between latency (L) and consistency (C)?

facts.claim: PA/EL systems like Dynamo give up consistency for availability during a partition, and give up consistency for latency in normal operation
facts.quote: upon a partition, they give up consistency for availability; and under normal operation they give up consistency for lower latency.

facts.claim: PC/EC systems (fully ACID databases) refuse to give up consistency and pay both the availability and latency costs to achieve it
facts.quote: They refuse to give up consistency, and will pay the availability and latency costs to achieve it.

facts.claim: PC/EL systems like Yahoo's PNUTS give up consistency for latency in normal operation but do not give up additional consistency during a partition (they give up availability instead)
facts.quote: In normal operation they give up consistency for latency; however, upon a partition they don't give up any additional consistency (rather they give up availability).

facts.claim: Systems that give up consistency for availability during partitions also tend to give up consistency for latency absent partitions, which is what CAP alone fails to explain
facts.quote: systems that tend to give up consistency for availability when there is a partition also tend to give up consistency for latency when there is no partition

sources.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
sources.authority: The standard graduate-level textbook synthesizing replication, partitioning, transactions, consistency, batch/stream processing into one coherent framework; content-standards-mandated grounding for Part A. Table of contents page returned 403 to automated fetch; citations should reference chapter numbers from the well-known 1st-edition structure (Replication ch.5, Partitioning ch.6, Transactions ch.7, Consistency and Consensus ch.9, Batch Processing ch.10, Stream Processing ch.11) until a writer can access a preview copy to confirm 2nd-edition renumbering.

sources.title: BeyondCorp: Design to Deployment at Google
sources.authors: Barclay Osborn, Justin McWilliams, Betsy Beyer, Max Saltonstall
sources.authority: Primary Google paper on BeyondCorp, the origin of the 'zero trust' architecture pattern now standard in enterprise and platform security design.

facts.claim: BeyondCorp gates access to applications based on device state and user identity rather than physical location or network, treating both internal and external networks as completely untrusted
facts.quote: BeyondCorp doesn't gate access to services and tools based on a user's physical location or the originating network; instead, access policies are based on information about a device, its state, and its associated user. BeyondCorp considers both internal networks and external networks to be completely untrusted

facts.claim: The core components are the Trust Inferer, Device Inventory Service, Access Control Engine, Access Policy, Gateways, and Resources
facts.quote: the fundamental components of the BeyondCorp system include the Trust Inferer, Device Inventory Service, Access Control Engine, Access Policy, Gateways, and Resources.

facts.claim: The Trust Inferer continuously analyzes and annotates device state, setting the maximum trust tier a device may access and downgrading trust on missing security patches or infection signals
facts.quote: The Trust Inferer is a system that continuously analyzes and annotates device state. The system sets the maximum trust tier accessible by the device... If the operating system is missing some noncritical patches... trust can be downgraded to an intermediate tier

facts.claim: Resources are accessed only via gateways (SSH servers, web proxies, 802.1x-enabled networks) that enforce a minimum trust tier or assign a VLAN
facts.quote: Resources are accessed via Gateways, such as SSH servers, Web proxies, or 802.1x-enabled networks. Gateways perform authorization actions, such as enforcing a minimum trust tier or assigning a VLAN.

facts.claim: Google's Device Inventory Service ingested billions of deltas from over 15 data sources at roughly three million per day, totaling over 80 terabytes
facts.quote: we've ingested billions of deltas from over 15 data sources, at a typical rate of about three million per day, totaling over 80 terabytes.

sources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, Chapter 4: Service Level Objectives
sources.authors: Chris Jones, John Wilkes, Niall Murphy, Cody Smith (ed. Betsy Beyer)
sources.authority: Google's own canonical definitions of SLI/SLO/SLA, the vocabulary content-standards requires for the observability/SLO module.

facts.claim: An SLI is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided
facts.quote: An SLI is a service level indicator—a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service that is provided.

facts.claim: An SLO is a target value or range for a service level measured by an SLI
facts.quote: An SLO is a service level objective: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by an SLI.

facts.claim: An SLA is an explicit or implicit contract with consequences for meeting or missing the SLOs it contains; missing an SLO without consequence means it was only an SLO, not an SLA
facts.quote: SLAs are service level agreements: an explicit or implicit contract with your users that includes consequences of meeting (or missing) the SLOs they contain... An easy way to tell the difference between an SLO and an SLA is to ask 'what happens if the SLOs aren't met?': if there is no explicit consequence, then you are almost certainly looking at an SLO.

facts.claim: Example SLI/SLO: 99% (averaged over 1 minute) of Get RPC calls will complete in less than 100ms
facts.quote: 99% (averaged over 1 minute) of Get RPC calls will complete in less than 100 ms

facts.claim: Google Compute Engine's published availability target is 'three and a half nines' -- 99.95%
facts.quote: Google Compute Engine availability is 'three and a half nines'—99.95% availability

sources.title: Netflix/Hystrix wiki: How it Works

sources.authority: Netflix's own documentation of Hystrix, the circuit-breaker/bulkhead library that popularized the resilience patterns (timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fallbacks) now standard in service-mesh and gateway layers.

facts.claim: Hystrix isolates points of access to remote systems to stop cascading failure and enable resilience where failure is inevitable
facts.quote: Hystrix is a latency and fault tolerance library designed to isolate points of access to remote systems, services and 3rd party libraries, stop cascading failure and enable resilience in complex distributed systems where failure is inevitable.

facts.claim: The circuit breaker trips from CLOSED to OPEN once request volume exceeds circuitBreakerRequestVolumeThreshold and the error percentage exceeds circuitBreakerErrorThresholdPercentage; after circuitBreakerSleepWindowInMilliseconds it allows one trial request through in a HALF-OPEN state
facts.quote: Assuming the volume across a circuit meets a certain threshold... and the error percentage exceeds the threshold error percentage... the circuit-breaker transitions from CLOSED to OPEN... the next single request is let through (this is the HALF-OPEN state).

facts.claim: With thread-pool isolation, clients execute on separate threads so the calling thread (e.g. a Tomcat thread) can time out and walk away from a slow dependency
facts.quote: Clients (libraries, network calls, etc) execute on separate threads. This isolates them from the calling thread (Tomcat thread pool).

facts.claim: Semaphore isolation cannot enforce timeouts: if a semaphore-isolated dependency becomes latent, the parent thread stays blocked until the underlying network call itself times out
facts.quote: if a dependency is isolated with a semaphore and then becomes latent, the parent threads will remain blocked until the underlying network calls timeout... [semaphores] do not allow for timing out.

sources.title: Using nginx as HTTP load balancer
sources.authority: Official reference-implementation documentation for the four canonical load-balancing algorithms (round robin, least connections, ip-hash, weighted) at the reverse-proxy layer.

facts.claim: Round robin (the default) has no session affinity: each subsequent request from the same client can land on a different server
facts.quote: with round-robin or least-connected load balancing, each subsequent client's request can be potentially distributed to a different server. There is no guarantee that the same client will be always directed to the same server.

facts.claim: Least-connected (least_conn) sends new requests to whichever upstream server currently has the fewest active connections, avoiding overloading a slow busy server
facts.quote: With the least-connected load balancing, nginx will try not to overload a busy application server with excessive requests, distributing the new requests to a less busy server instead.

facts.claim: ip_hash uses the client IP as a hash key so a given client is always routed to the same server (except when that server is down), providing sticky sessions
facts.quote: With ip-hash, the client's IP address is used as a hashing key to determine what server in a server group should be selected for the client's requests. This method ensures that the requests from the same client will always be directed to the same server except when this server is unavailable.

facts.claim: A weight=3 directive on one server out of three sends 3 of every 5 requests to it (proportional weighted round robin)
facts.quote: With this configuration, every 5 new requests will be distributed across the application instances as the following: 3 requests will be directed to srv1, one request will go to srv2, and another one -- to srv3.

sources.title: Content Delivery Network (CDN) Reference Architecture
sources.authority: Official CDN architecture documentation from a major CDN operator, covering origin/edge/PoP topology, tiered caching, and TTL-based freshness/invalidation.

facts.claim: Cloudflare's edge network spans hundreds of cities worldwide, reaching 95% of the world's Internet-connected population within 50 milliseconds
facts.quote: spans hundreds of cities worldwide, reaching 95% of the world's Internet-connected population within 50 milliseconds.

facts.claim: With Tiered Cache, certain data centers act as reverse proxies to the origin for other data centers, increasing cache-hit rate and reducing origin load
facts.quote: With Tiered Cache, certain data centers are reverse proxies to the origin for other data centers, resulting in more cache hits and faster response times.

facts.claim: Cache Reserve adds a higher cache tier with longer retention using R2 object storage; when the TTL on content in Cache Reserve expires, the content must be revalidated against the origin
facts.quote: an additional higher tier of cache with longer retention duration... The TTL policy still affects the content's freshness which means when content cache TTL expires inside of Cache Reserve, the content will need to be revalidated by checking the origin for any updates.

sources.title: Resilient Distributed Datasets: A Fault-Tolerant Abstraction for In-Memory Cluster Computing
sources.authors: Matei Zaharia, Mosharaf Chowdhury, Tathagata Das, et al.
sources.authority: Primary paper introducing Spark/RDDs, the system that succeeded MapReduce for iterative and interactive workloads and the direct conceptual ancestor of the batch/stream lineage Aman's brief asks for.

facts.claim: RDDs achieve fault tolerance via lineage (recording the transformations used to build a dataset) rather than data replication or logging updates to mutable state
facts.quote: RDDs provide fault tolerance efficiently. If a partition of an RDD is lost, the RDD has enough information about how it was derived from other RDDs to recompute just that partition.

facts.claim: RDDs restrict writes to coarse-grained transformations (map, filter, join) rather than fine-grained updates to shared state, which is what makes cheap fault tolerance possible
facts.quote: RDDs can only be created ('written') through coarse-grained transformations, while DSM allows reads and writes to each memory location. This restricts RDDs to applications that perform bulk writes, but allows for more efficient fault tolerance.

facts.claim: Spark is up to 20x faster than Hadoop for iterative applications, speeds up a real-world data analytics report by 40x, and can scan a 1TB dataset interactively with 5-7s latency
facts.quote: We show that Spark is up to 20x faster than Hadoop for iterative applications, speeds up a real-world data analytics report by 40x, and can be used interactively to scan a 1 TB dataset with 5-7s latency.

facts.claim: RDDs let a user persist a dataset in memory across queries via a persist() call, avoiding recomputation when the same data is reused across operations
facts.quote: programmers can call a persist method to indicate which RDDs they want to reuse in future operations.

sources.title: What is Vitess?
sources.authority: Official documentation for Vitess, the MySQL-sharding middleware built at YouTube/Google and now run by Slack, Square, JD.com; the canonical citation for YouTube's database layer.

facts.claim: Vitess served all of YouTube's database traffic for over five years
facts.quote: Vitess served all YouTube database traffic for over five years.

facts.claim: VTGate is a proxy that accepts MySQL protocol connections and routes queries to the appropriate shards; VTTablet is an agent alongside each MySQL instance managing queries, connections, and replication
facts.quote: VTGate: A proxy that accepts MySQL protocol connections from your application and routes queries to the appropriate shards... VTTablet: An agent running alongside each MySQL instance that manages queries, connections, and replication.

facts.claim: A consistent data store (etcd, ZooKeeper, or Consul) maintains Vitess cluster topology state
facts.quote: Topology Service: A consistent data store (etcd, ZooKeeper, or Consul) that maintains the cluster state.

facts.claim: Each MySQL connection carries a memory overhead between 256KB and almost 3MB depending on release; Vitess is built to handle thousands of connections cheaply on top of that constraint
facts.quote: Every MySQL connection has a memory overhead that ranges between 256KB and almost 3MB, depending on which MySQL release you're using... Vitess can easily handle thousands of connections.

sources.title: Serving 100 Gbps from an Open Connect Appliance
sources.authority: Netflix's own account of the FreeBSD/NVMe engineering that lets a single CDN appliance saturate 100Gbps -- the numbers behind Open Connect, Netflix's purpose-built CDN.

facts.claim: The stated goal and eventual result was serving 100 Gbps from a single FreeBSD-based Open Connect Appliance using NVMe-based storage
facts.quote: serve at 100 Gbps from a single FreeBSD-based Open Connect Appliance... NVM Express (NVMe)-based storage

facts.claim: Progression of measured throughput across hardware/software iterations: 40 Gbps (CPU-limited, Xeon E5-2697v2) -> 52 Gbps (PCIe Gen3 x8-limited) -> ~70-80 Gbps (prototype hardware) -> over 90 Gbps first achieved -> 90 Gbps sustained with 100% TLS traffic
facts.quote: CPU limited serving at 40 Gbps using single-socket Xeon E5-2697v2... boosted our performance into the 70 Gbps range... serve at well over 90 Gbps for the first time... serve 100% TLS traffic comfortably at 90 Gbps

facts.claim: Serving entirely from memory rather than NVMe disk dropped performance from 40 Gbps CPU-limited to only 22 Gbps CPU-limited, an explicit memory-vs-disk trade-off
facts.quote: the performance actually dropped from being CPU limited at 40 Gbps to being CPU limited at only 22 Gbps

facts.claim: 10-20% of the most popular titles are served from memory; the rest from NVMe SSD, exploiting a long-tail content-popularity distribution
facts.quote: 10-20% of the most popular titles being served from memory

facts.claim: Detailed TCP statistics collection for every connection consumed 5-10% of CPU, so Netflix samples only a small percentage of connections
facts.quote: collecting detailed TCP statistics for every TCP connection consumed 5-10% of the CPU, addressed by sampling only a small percentage of connections

sources.title: Per-Title Encode Optimization

facts.quote: Netflix estimates about a 20% reduction in bitrates from the approach (and 30% by doing this on a per-scene basis)

sources.title: Principles of Chaos Engineering
sources.authors: Chaos Engineering community (originated by Netflix's Chaos Team)
sources.authority: The canonical published definition of chaos engineering, co-authored by the Netflix engineers who built Chaos Monkey and the Simian Army.

facts.claim: Chaos Engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system to build confidence in its capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production
facts.quote: Chaos Engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in the system's capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production.

facts.claim: Advanced principle: build a hypothesis around measurable steady-state output, not internal system attributes
facts.quote: Focus on the measurable output of a system, rather than internal attributes of the system.

facts.claim: Advanced principle: chaos experiments should run directly on production traffic to guarantee authenticity and relevance
facts.quote: To guarantee both authenticity of the way in which the system is exercised and relevance to the current deployed system, Chaos strongly prefers to experiment directly on production traffic.

facts.claim: Advanced principle: minimize blast radius -- some short-term negative impact is allowed but must be minimized and contained
facts.quote: While there must be an allowance for some short-term negative impact, it is the responsibility and obligation of the Chaos Engineer to ensure the fallout from experiments are minimized and contained.

sources.title: System Architectures for Personalization and Recommendation
sources.authors: Netflix Technology Blog (Justin Basilico, Xavier Amatriain, et al.)
sources.authority: Netflix's own account of its offline/nearline/online computation split for recommendations, the clearest published statement of that three-tier trade-off in the industry.

facts.claim: Netflix runs recommendation computation across three modes: offline (batch, no latency limit), nearline (event-driven, near real-time), and online (synchronous, request-time, latency-SLA-bound)
facts.quote: Online computation... can respond quickly to events and use the most recent data... Offline computation... allows for more choices in algorithmic approach... Nearline computation... can be seen as a compromise between the two previous modes

facts.claim: Online computation is explicitly bound by availability and response-time SLAs, which limits the complexity of algorithms that can run there
facts.quote: subject to an availability and response time Service Level Agreements (SLAs)... can make it harder to fit complex and computationally costly algorithms

facts.claim: Offline computation will not react quickly to new data, leading to staleness that can degrade the member experience
facts.quote: will not react quickly to changes in context or new data. Ultimately, this can lead to staleness that may degrade the member experience.

facts.claim: Manhattan is Netflix's internal near-real-time event-flow computation framework, described by Netflix as similar to Storm but addressing different concerns; Hermes is the internal pub/sub layer notifying subscribers when a query result is ready, supporting HDFS, S3, or Cassandra as backing stores
facts.quote: Manhattan... is somewhat similar to Twitter's Storm, but it addresses different concerns... Hermes... notifies subscribers when the result of a query is ready... supports different repositories (not only HDFS, but also S3 or Cassandra).

sources.title: Ingesting Live Video Streams at Global Scale
sources.authority: Twitch's own account of its live-ingest routing architecture (Intelligest, IRS, Capacitor, The Well), grounding the low-latency-live-video case study.

facts.quote: nearly a hundred points of presence (PoPs) in different geographic regions

facts.claim: Named components: an Intelligest media proxy in each PoP that terminates live streams and queries the routing service; the Intelligest Routing Service (IRS) running in AWS as the stateful controller; Capacitor monitoring compute-resource fluctuations at origins; The Well monitoring backbone network status/utilization
facts.quote: Intelligest media proxy running in each PoP... Intelligest Routing Service (IRS) running in AWS... Capacitor... monitors compute resources and capacity fluctuations in origins... The Well... monitors backbone network status, utilization, and availability

facts.claim: Twitch ingests RTMP and WebRTC and translates them to an internal canonical protocol across its backbone; PoPs previously used HAProxy for load balancing
facts.quote: RTMP and WebRTC as ingestible protocols... internal 'canonical' protocol across Twitch backbone... All the PoPs ran HAProxy - a free and open source load-balancing software

facts.quote: The computed routing solution is static and is not able to handle unexpected traffic patterns and system fluctuations in real time

sources.title: Twitch Engineering: An Introduction and Overview

facts.quote: We have over 30,000 people streaming video on Twitch simultaneously... We have peaked at over 2 million concurrent video streams on our site.

sources.title: 1 million is so 2011

facts.claim: WhatsApp pushed a single server to over 2 million concurrent TCP connections
facts.quote: we are now able to easily push our systems to over 2 million tcp connections!!

facts.claim: The server ran FreeBSD 8.2-STABLE amd64 with Erlang R14B03 (erts-5.8.4), 24 CPU cores, 103GB physical memory, on Intel Xeon X5675 @ 3.07GHz
facts.quote: FreeBSD 8.2-STABLE amd64... Erlang R14B03 (erts-5.8.4) [64-bit] [smp:24:24]... 24 CPU cores... 103GB physical memory... Intel Xeon X5675 @ 3.07GHz

facts.quote: kern.ipc.maxsockets=2400000; kern.maxfiles=3000000; kern.maxfilesperproc=2700000; net.inet.tcp.tcbhashsize=524288

sources.title: Sharding & IDs at Instagram
sources.authority: Instagram's own explanation of its Postgres logical-sharding scheme and 64-bit ID generation, the primary source for the Instagram storage case study. The origin domain refused direct connections (ECONNREFUSED) and reader-proxy retries returned errors, so facts below are drawn from the WebSearch tool's summary of the same page, not independently verified against full text.

facts.claim: Instagram evaluated NoSQL but chose to shard data across several thousand logical shards mapped onto far fewer physical PostgreSQL servers, using Postgres schemas to make this easy to script/administrate
facts.quote: several thousand 'logical' shards mapped to far fewer physical shards, allowing them to start with just a few database servers and eventually move to many more by moving logical shards without re-bucketing data. Instagram used Postgres' schemas feature

facts.claim: Instagram's custom 64-bit ID scheme allocates 41 bits to time, 13 bits to shard ID, and 10 bits to a per-shard sequence, generated via a PL/pgSQL function inside each shard
facts.quote: Instagram's custom 64-bit ID generation used PL/pgSQL functions within each shard with 41 bits for time, 13 bits for shard ID, and 10 bits for sequence.

sources.title: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency
sources.authority: Stripe's own explanation of idempotency keys, the payments-API pattern the request explicitly says the AI-billing module should reuse.

facts.claim: Stripe's mutating endpoints accept an Idempotency-Key header; a retried request with the same key returns the cached result of the first request, including cached 5xx errors
facts.quote: a client generates a unique ID to identify just that operation and sends it up to the server along with the normal payload... the server simply replies with a cached result of the successful operation

facts.claim: Stripe's own client libraries retry automatically on failure using an idempotency key with exponential backoff and jitter
facts.quote: The Stripe Ruby library retries on failure automatically with an idempotency key using increasing backoff times and jitter

facts.claim: A key that is currently in-flight is a distinct third state (neither absent nor complete); treating it as only two states turns a legitimate retry into a duplicate write
facts.quote: a key that is currently in flight is neither absent nor complete, and getting that wrong turns a retry into a duplicate

sources.title: H3: Uber's Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index
sources.authority: Uber's own explanation of H3, the geospatial indexing library it built and open-sourced for dispatch/pricing/ETA, and why hexagons beat squares/postal codes for this workload.

facts.claim: H3 supports sixteen resolutions; each finer resolution cell has one-seventh the area of the coarser resolution
facts.quote: H3 supports sixteen resolutions... each finer resolution containing cells having one seventh the area of the coarser resolution.

facts.claim: The globe is tiled from an icosahedron with 122 base cells (10 per face) and 12 unavoidable pentagons at the icosahedron vertices, since perfect hexagonal tiling of a sphere is impossible
facts.quote: 122 base cells over the Earth, with ten cells per face... Twelve pentagons, one at each of the icosahedron vertices are incorporated since perfect hexagonal tiling is impossible.

facts.claim: H3 indexes are 64-bit integers
facts.quote: 64-bit integers... or 64-bit H3 index

facts.claim: Hexagons have only one distance between a cell centerpoint and each neighbor, unlike squares which have two distinct neighbor distances requiring multiple coefficient sets; postal codes and operator-drawn zones have unstable, arbitrary shapes unsuitable for analysis
facts.quote: Squares have two different types of neighbors... hexagons have only one distance between a hexagon centerpoint and its neighbors... Postal areas exhibit unusual shapes and sizes which are not helpful for analysis, and are subject to change.

sources.title: Uber Engineering's Ringpop
sources.authority: Uber's own explanation of Ringpop, the SWIM-gossip/consistent-hashing library underlying application-layer sharding for its dispatch (DISCO) and geospatial services.

facts.claim: Ringpop implements a SWIM gossip protocol variant over TCP, computes membership/ring checksums, and retains down members in its member list
facts.quote: Ringpop 1) implements a SWIM gossip protocol variation, 2) gossips over TCP, 3) computes membership and ring checksums, and 4) retains members that are down in its member list.

facts.claim: Nodes repeatedly ping each other so every node learns of every other node's existence and status, letting work be divided automatically without a centralized coordinator
facts.quote: nodes...repeatedly ping each other so that each node knows about every other node's existence and status... the SWIM gossip membership protocol lets us divvy up work automatically.

facts.claim: Ringpop's consistent-hash ring uses FarmHash as its hash function and a red-black tree for the ring structure, with a uniform number of replica points added per node
facts.quote: Ringpop 1) uses FarmHash as its hashing function, 2) uses a red-black tree for its ring, and 3) adds a uniform number of replica points per node.

facts.claim: Because consistent hashing minimizes reassignment on membership change, adding/removing a node does not require rebalancing all object data, which reduces latency
facts.quote: you don't reassign and rebalance object data to new spots, significantly reducing latency.

sources.title: Building Services at Airbnb, Part 1

facts.quote: The Google Search index covers hundreds of billions of webpages and is over 100,000,000 gigabytes in size.
