facts.quote: The API uses the token bucket algorithm to do rate limiting. This means that your capacity is continuously replenished up to your maximum limit, rather than being reset at fixed intervals.

facts.claim: Monthly spend caps by tier: Start $500, Build $1,000, Scale $200,000; Custom tier has no cap
facts.quote: Start $500 USD; Build $1,000 USD; Scale $200,000 USD... Organizations on the Custom tier have no monthly spend cap

facts.claim: For most models, only uncached input tokens (input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens) count toward the ITPM rate limit; cache_read_input_tokens do not, so caching effectively raises throughput -- e.g. a 2,000,000 ITPM limit with an 80% cache hit rate can process ~10,000,000 total input tokens/minute
facts.quote: only uncached input tokens count toward your ITPM rate limits... With a 2,000,000 ITPM limit and an 80% cache hit rate, you could effectively process 10,000,000 total input tokens per minute

facts.claim: OTPM is evaluated in real time on actual tokens generated; the max_tokens request parameter does not count against OTPM, so setting it high carries no rate-limit downside
facts.quote: OTPM rate limits are evaluated in real time as output tokens are produced, counting only the actual tokens generated. The max_tokens parameter does not factor into OTPM rate limit calculations

facts.claim: Reaching the spend cap returns a 429 rate_limit_error with no retry-after header and an enforced_spend_limit_reached error_code, distinguishing it from an ordinary rate limit which always carries retry-after
facts.quote: The error type is rate_limit_error, the same as for a rate limit, but the response has no retry-after header... error.details.error_code is enforced_spend_limit_reached

facts.claim: Per-workspace rate limits can be set below the org-wide limit to protect other workspaces from overuse; unused workspace allocation is available to other workspaces, but the org-wide limit always applies even if workspace limits sum to more
facts.quote: you might limit one Workspace to 30,000 input tokens per minute. This protects other Workspaces... Organization-wide limits always apply, even if Workspace limits add up to more.

conflicts: OpenAI (S35) enforces rate limits primarily via fixed-window-like per-minute/per-day counters across 6 independent dimensions (RPM/RPD/TPM/TPD/IPM/audio); Anthropic (S36) uses a continuously-replenishing token bucket across 3 dimensions (RPM/ITPM/OTPM) and explicitly excludes cached tokens from the input-token count -- two different philosophies for the same generate-now-know-cost-later problem.

sources.title: Prompt caching (Claude API)
sources.authority: Anthropic's own mechanism description for prefix caching, including breakpoint semantics, TTL economics, and lookback window -- the primary source for the platform prefix-caching module.

facts.claim: Pricing multipliers: 5-minute cache write = 1.25x base input; 1-hour cache write = 2x base input; cache read = 0.1x base input (0.025x on some newer models)
facts.quote: 5-minute cache write tokens are 1.25 times the base input tokens price... 1-hour cache write tokens are 2 times the base input tokens price... Cache read tokens are 0.1 times the base input tokens price

facts.claim: A cache write is created only at an explicit breakpoint (a hash of the prefix ending there); reads walk backward up to 20 positions looking for a matching prefix hash written by a prior request
facts.quote: Marking a block with cache_control writes exactly one cache entry... If none exists, it walks backward one block at a time... The system checks at most 20 positions per breakpoint

facts.claim: Up to 4 explicit cache breakpoints are allowed per request; cache prefixes are built in order tools -> system -> messages, and a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it
facts.quote: You can define up to 4 cache breakpoints... Cache prefixes are created in the following order: tools, system, then messages... Changes at each level invalidate that level and all subsequent levels

facts.claim: Default cache lifetime is 5 minutes, measured from the start of the write/read request, not the end of the response -- a 4-minute-long response leaves only about 1 minute for a follow-up request to hit the cache
facts.quote: By default, the cache has a 5-minute lifetime... Time spent generating a response counts against the lifetime: if a response takes 4 minutes to stream, a follow-up request that reuses the same cached prefix must start within about 1 minute

facts.claim: For concurrent requests, a cache entry only becomes available after the first response begins, so parallel requests racing on a cold cache will all miss
facts.quote: a cache entry only becomes available after the first response begins. If you need cache hits for parallel requests, wait for the first response before sending subsequent requests.

facts.claim: Minimum cacheable prompt length varies from 512 tokens (some models) up to 4,096 tokens (others); shorter prompts marked cacheable are processed without caching and without error
facts.quote: Shorter prompts cannot be cached, even if marked with cache_control... 512 tokens: Claude Opus 5... 4,096 tokens: Claude Opus 4.5

sources.title: Prompt caching (OpenAI API)
sources.authority: OpenAI's own mechanism description for prompt caching (automatic, prefix-based, no explicit breakpoints) -- lets a writer contrast OpenAI's automatic-caching design against Anthropic's explicit-breakpoint design (S37).

facts.claim: OpenAI's cache lookup walks the longest-to-shortest prefix of the incoming request looking for a matching prefix already resident on a serving machine, rather than requiring an explicit cache_control marker
facts.quote: OpenAI walks through only the cache lookup boundaries in the incoming request, from longest prefix to shortest, looking for an available matching prefix already cached on the machine.

facts.claim: Cache reads are discounted up to 90%; on GPT-5.6+ minimum cacheable length is 1,024 tokens, cache writes cost 1.25x base rate and reads cost 0.1x base rate
facts.quote: discounted up to 90%... minimum cacheable prompt length is 1,024 tokens... Cache writes: 1.25x the standard, uncached input-token rate... Cache reads: only 0.1x that rate

facts.claim: On GPT-5.6+, a cache persists 30 minutes after its most recent write or reuse; earlier models retain caches roughly 5-10 minutes up to one hour (in-memory) or up to 24 hours (24h explicit mode)
facts.quote: 30 minutes after its most recent write or reuse... typically around 5 to 10 minutes of inactivity, up to one hour... around 30 minutes and can retain them for up to 24 hours

facts.claim: Manual cache clearing is not available, and cached input tokens still count toward tokens-per-minute rate limits -- an explicit contrast with Anthropic's exclusion of cached tokens from ITPM (S36)
facts.quote: Manual cache clearing is not currently available... Cached input tokens still count toward tokens-per-minute limits.

conflicts: OpenAI (S38) counts cached input tokens toward its TPM rate limit; Anthropic (S36/S37) explicitly excludes cache_read_input_tokens from ITPM for most models, meaning heavy cache use raises effective throughput headroom on Anthropic but not on OpenAI.

sources.title: Life of a Request (LiteLLM Proxy architecture)
sources.authority: LiteLLM's own architecture doc for its open-source LLM gateway/proxy -- the request explicitly names LiteLLM as a reference open-source gateway.

facts.claim: Request flow: virtual-key auth/budget check (cache lookup, DB fallback on miss) -> parallel-request rate limiter (rpm/tpm at global/key/user/team levels) -> LiteLLM Router (load balancing, fallbacks, retries) -> SDK translation to OpenAI format -> provider call
facts.quote: the Bearer token in the request is checked to ensure it is valid and under its budget... The parallel request limiter checks the rate limit (rpm/tpm)... The LiteLLM Router handles Load balancing, Fallbacks, Retries

facts.claim: After the response returns to the client, spend logging, rate-limit accounting, and logging callbacks all run as asynchronous background tasks -- no database write sits in the request's critical path
facts.quote: After the response is returned to the client, spend logging, rate-limit accounting, and logging callbacks all run as asynchronous background tasks; no database write sits in the request path.

facts.claim: Virtual keys support hard limits (tokens, requests, upstream-billing caps), soft limits with alerts, model whitelists, and per-key rate limits; spend is tracked per key, and if attached, rolls up to a user_id and team_id
facts.quote: Virtual keys can have hard limits (tokens, requests, upstream-billing caps), soft limits with alerts, model whitelists, and rate limits... spend for that user is tracked... team in the LiteLLM_TeamTable

sources.title: Usage-based Rate Limiting (Envoy AI Gateway / Agent Router docs)
sources.authors: Envoy AI Gateway project (rebranded 'Agent Router' in v0.1 docs)
sources.org: Envoy AI Gateway (CNCF-adjacent, backed by Tetrate/Bloomberg/others)
sources.authority: Envoy AI Gateway's own description of token-based rate limiting layered on Envoy's Global Rate Limit API -- the request explicitly names Envoy AI Gateway as a reference gateway.

facts.claim: The gateway automatically extracts token usage (input/output/total) from LLM responses that follow the OpenAI schema format, including via response transformers for non-OpenAI backends like AWS Bedrock
facts.quote: AI Gateway automatically extracts token usage from LLM responses that follow the OpenAI schema format... For model providers with OpenAI schema transformations like AWS Bedrock, AI Gateway automatically captures token usage through its request/response transformer

facts.claim: Enforcement is two-phase: on request arrival, the gateway checks whether processing would exceed the configured token limit and rejects with 429 if so; otherwise it processes the request and only then counts the resulting token usage toward the total
facts.quote: When a request is received: AI Gateway checks if processing this request would exceed the configured token limit. If the limit would be exceeded, the request is rejected with a 429 status code. If within the limit, the request is processed and its token usage is counted towards the total.

facts.claim: Custom cost metrics can be computed with CEL expressions, e.g. to weight cached tokens differently from live tokens
facts.quote: users can use Common Expression Language (CEL) to calculate custom cost metrics, useful for weighting cached tokens differently or implementing complex pricing models.

facts.claim: Example config limits: 1,000 total tokens/hour/user for GPT-4, 5,000 total tokens/hour/user for GPT-3.5-turbo
facts.quote: GPT-4: 1000 total tokens per hour per user... GPT-3.5-turbo: 5000 total tokens per hour per user

conflicts: Envoy AI Gateway (S40) admits a request before knowing its true token cost, then reconciles after the fact -- an optimistic-admission design distinct from Anthropic's estimate-then-adjust-during-the-request approach (S36).

sources.title: Introduction (Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension)
sources.authors: kubernetes-sigs contributors (Red Hat, Google Cloud, IBM Research, CoreWeave, NVIDIA)
sources.authority: Official docs for the Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension, the project explicitly named in the request as a reference open-source gateway for inference-aware routing.

facts.claim: An InferencePool represents a set of endpoints running a model-server framework; the Endpoint Picker (EPP) is the Inference Router implementation that fetches metrics from pool endpoints to pick the one that best meets configured objectives
facts.quote: InferencePools represent set of endpoints running a model server framework... EPP functions as an implementation of an Inference Router that will fetch metrics from whichever portion of the InferencePool endpoints can best achieve the configured objectives.

facts.claim: The architecture reuses Envoy's External Processing (ext-proc) protocol to extend any ext-proc-and-Gateway-API-capable gateway into an inference-aware gateway, rather than building a bespoke gateway
facts.quote: leveraging Envoy's External Processing Protocol to extend any gateway that supports both ext-proc and Gateway API into an inference gateway.

facts.claim: Model-server-aware, metrics-driven load balancing is claimed to reduce serving latency and improve accelerator utilization versus generic L7 balancing
facts.quote: Model Server-aware load balancing... has been proven to reduce the serving latency and improve utilization of accelerators in your clusters.

sources.title: Introducing Gateway API Inference Extension
sources.authority: The Kubernetes project's own announcement explaining why LLM inference traffic breaks generic HTTP load balancing.

facts.claim: LLM inference sessions are long-running, resource-intensive, and partially stateful -- a single GPU-backed model server may keep multiple sessions active with in-memory token caches, unlike typical short-lived stateless web requests
facts.quote: Unlike typical short-lived, stateless web requests, LLM inference sessions are often long-running, resource-intensive, and partially stateful. For example, a single GPU-backed model server may keep multiple inference sessions active and maintain in-memory token caches.

facts.claim: Traditional load balancers that route on HTTP path or round-robin lack model-identity and request-criticality awareness (e.g. interactive chat vs. batch), which the Inference Extension adds as first-class routing signals
facts.quote: Traditional load balancers focused on HTTP path or round-robin lack the specialized capabilities needed for these workloads. They also don't account for model identity or request criticality (e.g., interactive chat vs. batch jobs).

facts.claim: The named routing signals introduced are KV-cache utilization and queue depth on candidate model servers
facts.quote: KV cache utilization... Queue depth

sources.title: Rate limiting (Cloudflare AI Gateway)
sources.authority: Cloudflare's own description of fixed vs. sliding window rate limiting at the AI-gateway layer -- the request explicitly names Cloudflare as a reference AI gateway.

facts.claim: Fixed window resets at time boundaries (e.g. 12:00-12:10), so 10 requests at 12:09 plus 10 at 12:11 both succeed (20 total) even against a 10-per-10-minutes limit
facts.quote: the window is based on time, so there would be no more than x requests in a ten minute window... sending 10 requests at 12:09 and 10 requests at 12:11... all 20 requests would be successful

facts.claim: Sliding window evaluates the trailing time interval continuously, so the same 20-request burst across the 12:09/12:11 boundary would fail under a 10-per-10-minutes sliding limit
facts.quote: there would be no more than x requests in the last ten minutes... they would fail in a sliding window strategy since there were more than ten requests in the last ten minutes

facts.claim: Exceeding the configured rate returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests and the request is not processed
facts.quote: the server will respond with a 429 Too Many Requests status code and your request will not be processed.

conflicts: Cloudflare (S43) documents fixed-window rate limiting as materially weaker than sliding-window (allowing 2x burst at a window boundary) using the same 10-per-10-minute example -- a concrete, quantified version of the classic fixed-vs-sliding-window trade-off.

sources.title: Moderation (OpenAI API)
sources.authority: OpenAI's own moderation-classifier taxonomy and integration guidance -- the primary source for the safety/moderation pipeline module's classifier design.

facts.claim: The moderation endpoint classifies against 13 categories: harassment, harassment/threatening, hate, hate/threatening, illicit, illicit/violent, self-harm, self-harm/intent, self-harm/instructions, sexual, sexual/minors, violence, violence/graphic
facts.quote: harassment; harassment/threatening; hate; hate/threatening; illicit; illicit/violent; self-harm; self-harm/intent; self-harm/instructions; sexual; sexual/minors; violence; violence/graphic

facts.claim: The response returns a boolean flagged, per-category booleans, per-category confidence scores 0-1, and which input types (text/image) each category applied to
facts.quote: flagged (boolean); categories (dictionary with per-category boolean flags); category_scores (dictionary with confidence scores 0-1); category_applied_input_types

facts.claim: OpenAI explicitly recommends treating moderation scores as policy signals rather than an automatic blocking decision, and reviewing results before showing generated output to a user or acting on it
facts.quote: Treat moderation scores as signals for your application's policy, not as an automatic blocking decision... Review the moderation results before you show the output to a user or take downstream actions.

sources.title: Building safeguards for Claude
sources.authority: Anthropic's own description of its safety pipeline across policy, training, pre-deployment testing, and real-time enforcement -- lets a writer contrast a training-time-integrated safety design against OpenAI's classifier-only moderation API (S44).

facts.claim: The pipeline has four stages: policy development (Usage Policy, Unified Harm Framework, Policy Vulnerability Testing with external experts), training integration (fine-tuning teams shape model refusal behavior), pre-deployment testing (safety/risk/bias evaluations), and real-time detection/enforcement
facts.quote: Safeguards designs our Usage Policy... Safeguards works closely with our fine-tuning teams... Safety evaluations assessing Usage Policy adherence... We use a combination of automated systems and human review to detect harm and enforce our Usage Policy once models are deployed.

facts.claim: Classifiers are prompted or specially fine-tuned Claude models used to detect policy violations in real time
facts.quote: prompted or specially fine-tuned Claude models called 'classifiers,' which are designed to detect specific types of policy violations in real-time.

facts.claim: Pre-deployment risk assessments explicitly cover CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear) and cyber-harm domains as a distinct high-risk category from general safety evaluations
facts.quote: Risk assessments for high-risk domains including cyber harm, or chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear weapons

conflicts: OpenAI (S44) ships moderation as a separate scoring endpoint applied around generation and explicitly recommends against automatic blocking; Anthropic (S45) embeds safety classifiers throughout training and real-time enforcement as one continuous pipeline rather than a bolt-on filter.

sources.title: Usage-based billing / Recording usage for billing (Stripe)
sources.authority: Stripe's own architecture for usage-based billing (meters, meter events, async aggregation) -- the metering/billing pattern the request says the AI-billing module should reuse.

facts.claim: Metronome (a Stripe product) is the recommended path for new usage-based billing integrations, providing real-time metering, flexible pricing, and continuous running-balance tracking rather than invoice-time-only totals
facts.quote: Metronome, a Stripe product, is a usage-based billing platform that provides real-time metering, pricing, billing and reporting... tracks running balances and usage totals continuously, so you and your customers can see current usage at any point during the billing period, not just at invoice time.

facts.claim: The legacy Billing Meters path sends meter events to a Stripe endpoint and Stripe aggregates them at the end of the billing period; Stripe explicitly processes meter events asynchronously, so aggregated usage summaries may lag recently received events
facts.quote: you send meter events to the Stripe /v1/billing/meter_events endpoint and Stripe aggregates them at the end of the billing period... Stripe processes meter events asynchronously, so aggregated usage in meter event summaries and on upcoming invoices might not immediately reflect recently received meter events.

facts.claim: Metronome is positioned as more suitable than Billing Meters for products where customers generate large numbers of events per second or per day
facts.quote: Metronome is also built for high-volume ingest, making it more suitable for products where customers generate large numbers of events per second or per day.

sources.title: Fireworks AI Deep Dive: Inference at Scale (third-party summary of Fireworks' own claims)
sources.authors: GMI Cloud (summarizing Fireworks AI's public claims)
sources.org: Fireworks AI (claims as reported by a third party)
sources.authority: The request names Fireworks AI as a reference inference platform; a direct Fireworks AI engineering blog post with this level of detail could not be located and fetched in the time budget, so these figures are Fireworks' own public claims as relayed by a third party and should be re-verified against fireworks.ai's own blog before being cited as fact in a module.

facts.claim: Fireworks reportedly runs dedicated GPU clusters per model/customer tier rather than sharing GPU resources across customers, to avoid noisy-neighbor variance
facts.quote: unlike serverless providers that share GPU resources across multiple customers, Fireworks runs dedicated GPU clusters for each model and customer tier, eliminating the 'noisy neighbor' performance variations common in shared infrastructure

facts.claim: Fireworks reportedly processes 200,000 queries/second and 10+ trillion tokens/day at peak, across tens of GPU clouds, using a custom inference engine (FireAttention) with continuous batching, paged attention, and prefill disaggregation
facts.quote: at peak, processes 200,000 queries per second and 10+ trillion tokens per day... custom inference engines (FireAttention)... continuous batching, paged attention, prefill disaggregation, and pipelining

conflicts: If accurate, Fireworks' claimed per-customer dedicated-cluster model (isolation-first) is the opposite of the shared-pool-plus-virtual-key model that gateways like LiteLLM (S39) and Envoy AI Gateway (S40) are built around (utilization-first); this is a real fork in multi-tenancy philosophy worth verifying against a primary Fireworks source.

sources.title: Code execution tool (Claude API)
sources.authority: Anthropic's own specification of its hosted code-execution sandbox: resource limits, container lifecycle, networking posture, and pricing -- the most detailed public spec of an agent-harness sandbox from a frontier lab.

facts.claim: Each container runs Python 3.11 on a Linux x86_64 sandbox with 5 GiB RAM, 5 GiB disk, and 1 CPU
facts.quote: Python version: 3.11... Operating system: Linux-based container... Architecture: x86_64 (AMD64)... Memory: 5 GiB RAM; Disk space: 5 GiB workspace storage; CPU: 1 CPU

facts.claim: Internet access is completely disabled inside the container; no outbound network requests are permitted, so only pre-installed libraries (pandas, numpy, scipy, matplotlib, etc.) are available -- packages cannot be installed at runtime
facts.quote: Internet access: Completely disabled for security... The container has no internet access, so Claude can't download or install additional packages at runtime: only the pre-installed libraries are available.

facts.claim: Containers expire 30 days after creation; after about 5 minutes of inactivity a container is checkpointed and can be restored by sending its ID again within the 30-day window; an expired container returns an error and cannot be restored
facts.quote: Containers expire 30 days after creation. After about 5 minutes of inactivity a container is checkpointed, and sending a request with its ID inside the 30-day window restores it... A container that has expired can't be reused.

facts.claim: Without web search/fetch, code execution is billed by execution time (minimum 5 minutes per invocation), with 1,550 free hours/month per organization and $0.05/hour per container beyond that; execution time bills even if the tool isn't called when files are attached, since files preload onto the container
facts.quote: Execution time has a minimum of 5 minutes; Each organization receives 1,550 free hours of usage per month; Additional usage beyond 1,550 hours is billed at $0.05 USD per hour, per container; If files are included in the request, execution time is billed even if the tool is not called

facts.claim: Code execution is free (no execution-time charge) when used together with the web_search or web_fetch tools, beyond standard token costs
facts.quote: Code execution is free when used with web search or web fetch. When web_search_20260209 (or later) or web_fetch_20260209 (or later) is included in your API request, there are no additional charges for code execution tool calls beyond the standard input and output token costs.

facts.claim: A pause_turn stop reason signals the API paused a long-running turn; the caller can resubmit the response as-is to let Claude continue, or modify content to interrupt
facts.quote: The response might include a pause_turn stop reason, which indicates that the API paused a long-running turn. You may provide the response back as-is in a subsequent request to let Claude continue its turn

facts.claim: Container data (execution artifacts, uploaded files, outputs) is retained up to 30 days server-side; files pushed through the Files API persist until explicitly deleted
facts.quote: Container data, including execution artifacts, uploaded files, and outputs, is retained for up to 30 days... Files that code execution creates in the Files API... persist until explicitly deleted.

sources.title: Unlocking the Codex harness: how we built the App Server
sources.authority: OpenAI's own architectural account of the Codex agent harness (threads, sandboxing, MCP tool wiring) -- the primary requested source for the agent-harness-backends module; direct WebFetch returned HTTP 403 in this session, so facts below are drawn from the WebSearch tool's cached summary rather than the full page text.

facts.claim: The Codex App Server owns the agent loop and sandboxed execution; the harness is defined as the surrounding execution system that manages conversation state, streamed activity, and tool interaction, while applications own product context, business rules, and tools
facts.quote: The Codex app-server provides the agent loop and sandboxed execution, while applications own product context, business rules, and tools. The harness handles the agent loop, conversation state, streamed activity, and tool interaction

facts.claim: A thread is a Codex conversation between a user and an agent; Codex creates, resumes, forks, and archives threads and persists their event history
facts.quote: a thread is a Codex conversation between a user and an agent, and Codex creates, resumes, forks, and archives threads, and persists the event history.

facts.claim: A useful harness must preserve/resume long-running work, decide what context to retain or compact, discover and validate tools, execute inside a sandbox, stream observable events, pause for approval, recover after interruption, and verify outcomes -- stated as the harness's core responsibility list
facts.quote: A useful harness has to preserve and resume long-running work, decide what context to retain or compact, discover and validate tools, execute inside a sandbox, stream observable events, pause for approval, recover after interruption, and verify outcomes.

sources.title: Streaming API responses (OpenAI API)
sources.authority: OpenAI's own SSE event taxonomy and an explicit stated limitation on moderating streamed output -- grounds the streaming-protocol module.

facts.claim: The Responses API streams typed lifecycle events over SSE: response.created, response.in_progress, response.output_text.delta, response.completed, response.failed, plus per-item events for function calls, code interpreter, and file search
facts.quote: ResponseCreatedEvent | ResponseInProgressEvent | ResponseFailedEvent | ResponseCompletedEvent | ResponseOutputItemAdded | ... ResponseFunctionCallArgumentsDelta | ResponseFunctionCallArgumentsDone | ResponseCodeInterpreterCallCodeDelta

facts.claim: Streaming output makes moderation harder because partial completions are harder to evaluate than a full response; if moderation scores are requested, they only arrive after the full output is generated and are not included with partial deltas
facts.quote: streaming the model's output in a production application makes it more difficult to moderate the content of the completions, as partial completions may be more difficult to evaluate... the scores arrive after the full generated output is available. They aren't included with partial output deltas.

sources.title: Background mode (OpenAI API)
sources.authority: OpenAI's own mechanism for stream resumption after a client disconnect -- directly grounds the request's 'resumption' requirement in the streaming module.

facts.claim: A response created with both background:true and stream:true can be resumed after a disconnect: the client tracks the sequence_number from each streamed event and reconnects with GET /v1/responses/{id}?stream=true&starting_after={sequence_number}
facts.quote: You will want to keep track of a 'cursor' corresponding to the sequence_number you receive in each streaming event... curl 'https://api.openai.com/v1/responses/resp_123?stream=true&starting_after=42'

facts.claim: Resumption is only possible if the background response was originally created with stream=true
facts.quote: You can only start a new stream from a background response if you created it with stream=true.

facts.claim: Response data is temporarily stored to disk for roughly 10 minutes to support asynchronous execution and polling
facts.quote: Response data is temporarily stored to disk for roughly 10 minutes to enable asynchronous execution and polling.

sources.title: Clio: Privacy-preserving insights into real-world AI use
sources.authority: Anthropic's own account of Clio, the production system it uses to analyze real conversation data for safety/observability while preserving privacy -- directly grounds the data-privacy-retention and LLM-observability modules' treatment of conversation-log analysis.

facts.claim: Clio was used to analyze 1 million claude.ai conversations across Free and Pro tiers; web/mobile app development was the top category at over 10% of conversations, education over 7%, business strategy nearly 6%
facts.quote: We used Clio to analyze 1 million conversations with Claude on claude.ai (both the Free and Pro tiers)... 'Web and mobile application development' category: over 10% of all conversations... Education: more than 7%... Business: nearly 6%

facts.claim: Clio's pipeline has four stages: extracting facets (topic/language metadata), semantic clustering by theme, cluster description with private information excluded, and building hierarchies for exploration; a minimum user/conversation threshold prevents small clusters (which might identify individuals) from surfacing
facts.quote: Extracting facets... Semantic clustering... Cluster description -- summaries excluding private information... Building hierarchies... Minimum threshold for the number of unique users or conversations, so that low-frequency topics... aren't inadvertently exposed

facts.claim: Claude itself verifies that cluster summaries do not contain overly specific or identifying information before they are shown to human analysts, and only these higher-level clusters -- not raw conversations -- are visible to analysts
facts.quote: Data are automatically anonymized and aggregated, and only the higher-level clusters are visible to human analysts... Claude verifies that cluster summaries don't contain any overly specific or identifying information before they're displayed

facts.claim: Clio's classification correlated with the separate Trust and Safety classification system at r = 0.71, and was used operationally to find false positives/negatives in that safety system and to detect a coordinated spam network using similar prompt structures
facts.quote: The overall correlation between the Trust and Safety and the Clio classifications was r = 0.71... Identified a network of automated accounts using similar prompt structures to generate spam for search engine optimization

sources.title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models
sources.authority: Meta's own paper describing the hardware, storage, network topology, reliability data, and post-training pipeline that powered Llama 3 405B pre-training -- the single most detailed public account of frontier-scale training infrastructure, explicitly named as required grounding in the request.

facts.claim: Llama 3 405B trains on up to 16K H100 GPUs (700W TDP, 80GB HBM3 each) on Meta's Grand Teton platform, 8 GPUs + 2 CPUs per server, connected via NVLink within a server; jobs are scheduled with MAST, Meta's global-scale training scheduler
facts.quote: Llama 3 405B is trained on up to 16K H100 GPUs, each running at 700W TDP with 80GB HBM3, using Meta's Grand Teton AI server platform. Each server is equipped with eight GPUs and two CPUs... Training jobs are scheduled using MAST, Meta's global-scale training scheduler.

facts.claim: Storage runs on Tectonic, Meta's general-purpose distributed file system, built on 7,500 SSD-equipped servers offering 240PB of storage, 2TB/s sustainable throughput and 7TB/s peak; per-GPU checkpoint state ranges 1MB-4GB and must be written during highly bursty checkpoint writes that saturate the storage fabric for short durations
facts.quote: Tectonic..., Meta's general-purpose distributed file system, is used to build a storage fabric for Llama 3 pre-training. It offers 240 PB of storage out of 7,500 servers equipped with SSDs, and supports a sustainable throughput of 2 TB/s and a peak throughput of 7 TB/s... Checkpointing saves each GPU's model state, ranging from 1 MB to 4 GB per GPU.

facts.claim: The RoCE-based 24K-GPU cluster uses a three-layer Clos network: 16 GPUs per rack (2 servers) behind a single ToR switch; 192 racks form a pod of 3,072 GPUs with full bisection bandwidth; 8 pods form the 24K-GPU cluster via aggregation switches at a 1:7 oversubscription ratio
facts.quote: our RoCE-based AI cluster comprises 24K GPUs connected by a three-layer Clos network... each rack hosts 16 GPUs... 192 such racks are connected by Cluster Switches to form a pod of 3,072 GPUs with full bisection bandwidth... eight such pods within the same datacenter building are connected via Aggregation Switches to form a cluster of 24K GPUs... has an oversubscription ratio of 1:7

facts.claim: 4D parallelism (tensor, pipeline, context, data/FSDP) is ordered [TP, CP, PP, DP] from innermost (highest bandwidth need) to outermost (most latency-tolerant); achieved BF16 MFU is 38-43% across the 8K/16K-GPU pre-training configurations

sources.authors: Hugging Face (author team synthesizing the RL-infra ecosystem)
sources.authority: The single most direct comparison available of trainer/rollout decoupling strategies across the RL-infra ecosystem, explicitly surveying verl, NeMo-RL, SkyRL, AReaL, and slime (four of the request's six named frameworks) side by side plus 11 others.

facts.claim: The dominant architecture disaggregates inference and training GPUs into two pools connected by a weight-synchronization protocol: an inference pool running vLLM/SGLang continuously and a training pool running the optimizer continuously
facts.quote: The inference pool runs vLLM or SGLang continuously; the training pool runs the optimizer continuously. The two pools communicate via a weight synchronisation protocol.

facts.claim: Staleness-management strategies fall into three orthogonal categories: hard version-rejection of samples too far behind current policy, depth-bounding via a fixed-capacity queue between generation and training, and importance-sampling correction (often clipped/truncated) for stale samples that do get used
facts.quote: Version rejection: Samples whose version falls behind the current policy by more than a threshold are hard-dropped... Depth bounding: The queue or buffer between generation and training has a bounded capacity... Importance sampling correction: Stale samples that reach the trainer are reweighted by the importance sampling ratio, typically clipped (Truncated IS).

facts.claim: 8 of the 16 surveyed frameworks (verl, SkyRL, NeMo-RL, SLIME, MILES, ROLL, OAT, open-instruct) use Ray for orchestration; verifiers-rl, PipelineRL, ART, and AReaL instead use native Python asyncio/threading; Atropos uses HTTP microservices; TorchForge uses the Monarch actor model
facts.quote: Ray-based (8/16 libraries): verl, SkyRL, NeMo-RL, SLIME, MILES, ROLL, OAT, open-instruct... Native Python (asyncio/threading): verifiers-rl, PipelineRL, ART, AReaL... HTTP microservices: Atropos... Monarch actor model: TorchForge

facts.claim: Weight-sync latency ranges from ~100-500ms for standard NCCL broadcast down to ~20ms with bucketing strategies; PipelineRL is unique in swapping weights between forward passes with only a ~1-10ms gap, never interrupting an in-flight sequence
facts.quote: NCCL Broadcast (standard)... latencies documented as '~100-500ms'... '~20ms' when libraries implement bucketing strategies... PipelineRL is described as unique...'sequences are never interrupted. Weights swap between forward passes (~1-10ms gap).'

facts.claim: For a 32B model generating 32K tokens/rollout across 512 sequences on a single H100 at ~1.2K tok/s, generation alone takes about 3.7 hours -- the concrete numeric illustration of why the generation step, not training, is the bottleneck that motivates async RL infra
facts.quote: For a 32B model generating 32K tokens per rollout across 512 sequences: time on 1xH100 (32B @ ~1.2K tok/s) = ~3.7 hours

conflicts: The survey (S63) documents three genuinely different staleness-tolerance philosophies in production RL frameworks (hard rejection, bounded depth, importance-sampling correction) rather than one converged answer, and a further fork between Ray-based (8/16) and native-async (4/16) orchestration -- both are live, unsettled design choices rather than solved problems.

sources.title: Applying Deep Learning To Airbnb Search
sources.authors: Malay Haldar, Mustafa Abdool, Prashant Ramanathan, Tao Xu, Shulin Yang, Huizhong Duan, Qing Zhang, Nick Barrow-Williams, Bradley C. Turnbull, Brendan M. Collins, Thomas Legrand
sources.authority: Airbnb's own account of replacing its gradient-boosted-decision-tree search-ranking model with a deep neural network, including the model-evolution sequence, feature engineering, and failed attempts; primary paper for the search-ranking case study.

facts.claim: Replacing the manually crafted scoring function with a GBDT model gave one of the largest step improvements in home bookings in Airbnb's history; the gains eventually saturated with long spells of neutral experiments
facts.quote: Replacing the manual scoring function with a gradient boosted decision tree (GBDT) model gave one of the largest step improvements in homes bookings in Airbnb's history, with many successful iterations to follow. The gains in online bookings eventually saturated with long spells of neutral experiments.

facts.claim: The first NN shipped to production was a single hidden layer network with 32 fully connected ReLU activations, fed the same features as the GBDT model and trained with L2 regression loss; it proved booking-neutral against GBDT
facts.quote: The first architecture that we finally managed to get online was a simple single hidden layer NN with 32 fully connected ReLU activations that proved booking neutral against the GBDT model.

facts.claim: The next model combined a NN with LambdaRank: a pairwise preference formulation over {booked, not-booked} listing pairs, with each pairwise loss weighted by the resulting change in NDCG from swapping the pair's rank positions
facts.quote: Our first breakthrough came when we combined a NN with the idea behind Lamdarank... Weighing each pairwise loss by the difference in NDCG resulting from swapping the positions of the two listings making up the pair.

facts.claim: A subsequent model combined GBDT leaf-node indices and a factorization-machine (FM) booking-probability prediction as additional input features into the NN
facts.quote: For the FM model we took the final prediction as a feature into the NN. From the GBDT model, we took the index of the leaf node activated per tree as a categorical feature.

facts.claim: The final production model was a deep NN with 2 hidden layers (127 and 83 ReLUs) fed by 195 input features after expanding categorical features to embeddings, reached by scaling training data 10x instead of adding architectural complexity
facts.quote: we were able to deprecate all that complexity by simply scaling the training data 10x and moving to a DNN with 2 hidden layers... an input layer with a total of 195 features... feeding the first hidden layer with 127 fully connected ReLUs, and then the second hidden layer with 83 fully connected ReLUs.

facts.claim: Training on 1.7 billion pairs closed the generalization gap between training and test NDCG for the DNN
facts.quote: Training on 1.7 billion pairs, we were able to close the generalization gap between the training and the test data set.

facts.claim: Using listing id as a learned embedding feature mostly led to overfitting (good training-set NDCG, no test-set gain) because even the most popular listing can be booked at most 365 times a year, unlike words or videos which can repeat without limit
facts.quote: in the different variations we tried, listing ids mostly led to overfitting... Even the most popular listing can be booked at most 365 times in an entire year. Typical bookings per listing are much fewer. This fundamental limitation generates data that is very sparse at the listing level.

facts.claim: A multi-task model predicting both booking and long-view probability with a shared listing-id embedding increased long views by a large margin online but left bookings neutral
facts.quote: When tested online, the model increased long views by a large margin. But bookings remained neutral.

facts.claim: Feeding raw GBDT-era features directly into the NN caused training loss to saturate; the fix was restricting features to a small numeric range (median mapped to 0, bulk of distribution in {-1,1}) via z-score normalization for normal-like distributions or log((1+x)/(1+median)) for power-law distributions
facts.quote: The loss would saturate in the middle of training... To avoid it we ensure all features are restricted to a small range of values, with the bulk of the distribution in the {-1, 1} interval and the median mapped to 0.

facts.claim: A high-cardinality categorical feature was built by hashing the query city together with the listing's level-12 S2 cell into an integer, then mapping that integer to a learned embedding, replacing a heavily engineered hierarchical neighborhood-distribution pipeline
facts.quote: given the query ”San Francisco” and a listing near the Embarcadero, we take the S2 cell the listing is situated in (539058204), and hash {”San Francisco”, 539058204} → 71829521 to build our categorical feature.

facts.claim: Switching the training pipeline from CSV/feed_dict to Protobuf/TensorFlow Dataset gave a 17x training speedup and raised GPU utilization from about 25% to about 90%
facts.quote: We were effectively towing a Ferrari with a mule... Retooling the pipeline to produce training data as Protobufs and using Dataset gave a 17x speedup to training and drove GPU utilization to ∼90%.

facts.claim: Two years after taking the first steps toward neural networks in search ranking, Airbnb frames deep learning as one of its biggest machine-learning success stories, having replaced feature engineering effort with system-scaling effort
facts.quote: moving to deep learning is not a drop-in model replacement at all; rather it's about scaling the system... Two years after taking the first steps towards applying neural networks to search ranking, we feel we are just getting started.

sources.title: Listing Embeddings in Search Ranking
sources.authors: Mihajlo Grbovic, Haibin Cheng, Qing Zhang, Lynn Yang, Phillippe Siclait, Matt Jones
sources.version: published 2018-03-13; companion post to Grbovic & Cheng, Real-time Personalization using Embeddings for Search Ranking at Airbnb, KDD 2018 (pp. 311-320)
sources.authority: Written by the KDD 2018 paper's own authors, this is Airbnb's own detailed account of the listing-embedding technique (skip-gram-style training over click sessions) that the KDD paper describes, including the exact training modifications, scale, and A/B-test results not reproduced in the paper's abstract.

facts.claim: Search Ranking and Similar Listings together drive 99% of Airbnb's booking conversions
facts.quote: Together, Search Ranking and Similar Listings drive 99% of our booking conversions.

facts.claim: Listing embeddings are 32-dimensional vectors learned from click sessions (a session ends after a 30-minute gap between clicks), chosen as a trade-off between offline performance and the RAM needed to hold vectors on search machines for real-time similarity calculation
facts.quote: the aim is to learn a 32-dimensional real-valued representation v(Li) of each unique listing... The dimensionality of the listing embeddings was set to d=32, as we found that to be a good trade-off between offline performance and the memory needed to store vectors in RAM memory of search machines.

facts.claim: Training uses negative sampling over a sliding window of length m=5: the central listing's vector is pushed toward positive context listings (clicked before/after within the window) and away from randomly sampled negative listings
facts.quote: listings that were clicked by the same user before and after central listing, within a window of length m (m = 5), and pushing it away from negative context listings: randomly sampled listings

facts.claim: Two modifications were added to the base skip-gram objective: the booked listing is kept as a global context term for every step in the session regardless of window position, and explicit market-level negative sampling is added because random negatives are almost never from the same market as the central listing, which otherwise degrades within-market similarity
facts.quote: the booked listing always remains within it as global context... We found that this imbalance leads to learning sub-optimal within-market similarities. To address this issue we propose to add a set of random negatives Dmn, sampled from the market of the central listing.

facts.claim: Embeddings were learned for 4.5 million active listings using more than 800 million search click sessions
facts.quote: Using the described optimization procedure we learned listing embeddings for 4.5 million active listings on Airbnb using more than 800 million search clicks sessions.

facts.claim: New listings without training data get a cold-start embedding computed as the mean vector of the 3 geographically closest listings of the same listing type and price range
facts.quote: To create embeddings for a new listing we find 3 geographically closest listings that do have embeddings, and are of same listing type and price range as the new listing, and calculate their mean vector.

facts.claim: An A/B test of embedding-based similar-listing recommendations (k=12 nearest neighbors by cosine similarity, filtered to the same market and available dates) increased the Similar Listing carousel's click-through rate by 21% and increased the share of guests discovering the listing they booked via that carousel by 4.9%
facts.quote: The A/B test showed that embedding-based solution lead to a 21% increase in Similar Listing carousel CTR and 4.9% more guests discovering the listing they ended up booking in the Similar Listing carousel.

facts.claim: Real-time personalization computes two similarity features per candidate listing from a Kafka-maintained rolling history of the last 2 weeks: similarity to recently clicked listings (EmbClickSim) and similarity to recently skipped listings (EmbSkipSim); these were added as ranking-model features and launched to production in Summer 2017
facts.quote: we collect and maintain in real-time (using Kafka) two sets of short-term history events... launch of embedding features for real-time personalization to production in Summer of 2017.

sources.title: Improving Deep Learning For Airbnb Search
sources.authors: Malay Haldar, Prashant Ramanathan, Tyler Sax, Mustafa Abdool, Lanbo Zhang, Aamir Mansawala, Shulin Yang, Bradley Turnbull, Junshuo Liao
sources.authority: Airbnb's own follow-up paper on the three post-launch problems (architecture, positional bias, cold start) it found after shipping the deep-learning ranker described in S67; primary source for the search-ranking case study's reported online A/B-test deltas.

facts.claim: Simply adding layers, residual connections, or batch normalization to the fully-connected DNN produced neutral offline NDCG; two hidden layers were sufficient and model capacity was not the bottleneck
facts.quote: Trying to decipher why increasing layers was not showing any gains led us to borrow more ideas from the literature, like applying residual learning and batch normalization. Still, NDCG refused to budge in offline tests... two hidden layers were sufficient and model capacity was not our problem.

facts.claim: Removing price as a direct DNN input and instead adding a separate monotonically-decreasing tanh(price) term to the output score dropped average search-result price by -5.7% online but dropped bookings by -1.5%, because isolating price from the rest of the model caused underfitting
facts.quote: average price of search results dropped by -5.7%, in confirmation with offline analysis... bookings dropped by -1.5%. Our hypothesis was that price interacted heavily with other features.

facts.claim: A generalized-monotonicity architecture (squared weights enforcing a monotonic price path plus an unconstrained subnet) tested online produced a similar booking drop of -1.6%, showing that strict price monotonicity was too strong a constraint
facts.quote: when tested online the results were very similar, resulting in a booking drop of -1.6%... The failure of this architecture suggested that monotonicity with regard to price was too strict a constraint.

facts.claim: A soft-monotonicity variant (price treated as an auxiliary pairwise loss term with a tunable weight alpha, chosen offline to match baseline NDCG) reduced average price by -3.3% online but still dropped bookings by -0.67%, revealing that the online full-inventory effect differed from the offline top-results-only re-ranking evaluation
facts.quote: we observed a reduction of -3.3% in average price of search results. But also a drop of -0.67% in bookings. The offline analysis suffered from the limitation that it only evaluated re-ranking the top results available in logs.

facts.claim: Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) plots showed the original fully-connected two-layer DNN already understood cheaper-is-better; the failed architectures were compromising result quality by forcing prices down further than the model itself preferred
facts.quote: The plots suggested that the fully connected two layer DNN... already understood cheaper was better... the failed architectures were compromising on quality.

facts.claim: A two-tower architecture (separate query/user tower and listing tower, each producing a 100-d vector, scored by Euclidean distance) increased bookings by +0.6% and online NDCG by +0.7% against the fully-connected two-layer DNN, with average search-result price dropping -2.3% as a side effect and overall revenue increasing +0.75%
facts.quote: the two tower architecture recorded a bookings gain of +0.6%... the NDCG computed online improved by +0.7%... we observed a drop of -2.3% in average price of search results... resulting in an overall increase of +0.75%.

facts.claim: Because the query/user tower does not depend on the listing, it can be scored once per search instead of once per listing; this reduced first-hidden-layer complexity from O(N*H*(Q+L)) to O(N*Hl*L + Hq*Q) and cut 99th-percentile scoring latency by -33% online
facts.quote: The computational complexity of the first hidden layer reduced to O(N * Hl * L + Hq * Q)... When tested online this resulted in a -33% reduction in the 99th percentile scoring latency.

facts.claim: NDCG for newly-listed properties was 6% lower than for established listings; removing all historical-engagement input features (past bookings, clicks, reviews) from the DNN entirely dropped overall NDCG by 4.5%, showing the DNN relies heavily on engagement features that new listings do not yet have
facts.quote: we observed a gap of -6%... Removal of these engagement features resulted in a drop of -4.5% in NDCG. Clearly, the DNN was relying heavily on engagement features.

facts.claim: An explicit ranking boost for new listings was tuned online to be bookings-neutral while allocating +8.5% additional first-page impressions to new listings
facts.quote: we tuned the new listing ranking boost to be bookings neutral compared to no boosting, while allocating +8.5% additional first page impressions to new listings.

facts.claim: Reframing cold start as estimating a new listing's future engagement features (via geographic-neighbor averaging matched on guest capacity) reduced offline engagement-estimation error by -42% versus using manually crafted default values, and in an online A/B test increased bookings of newly created listings by +14%, increased their first-page impression share by +14%, and increased overall bookings by +0.38%
facts.quote: the engagement estimator described above reduced engagement estimation error by -42%... we observed an improvement of +14% in bookings of newly created listings, along with a +14% increase in share of impressions of first page results... overall bookings increased by +0.38%.

facts.claim: Adding position as a DNN input feature, regularized away from the relevance prediction via a dropout rate of 0.15 (set to 0 at scoring time), increased bookings by +0.7%, lifted revenue by +1.8%, and increased bookings for boutique hotels/B&Bs by +1.1%, in an online A/B test against the same DNN with no notion of positional bias
facts.quote: we observed a gain of +0.7% in bookings... a lift of +1.8% in revenue was a pleasant surprise... we observed a +1.1% increase in bookings for boutique hotels.

facts.claim: Naively adding position as an input feature without dropout regularization dropped relevance-only NDCG (position fixed to 0 at test time) by about -1.3%, because the model learned to depend on the position feature during training in a way it could not use at scoring time
facts.quote: Comparing the NDCG of the DNN with position as feature to the baseline without the position feature, we see a drop of around -1.3%. So a straightforward introduction of the position as a control variable seem to hurt the relevance prediction.

sources.title: Avoiding double payments in a distributed payments system
sources.authority: Airbnb's own account of Orpheus, the idempotency library built to keep its SOA-based payments system from double-charging guests or double-paying hosts; the primary source for the booking/payments consistency case study.

facts.claim: An API call to a service that makes further calls to downstream services, each changing state with side effects, is equivalent to executing a complex distributed transaction; without a protocol such as two-phase commit, distributed transactions in an SOA present challenges to data integrity
facts.quote: An API call to a service that makes further API calls to downstream services, where each service changes state and potentially has side effects, is equivalent to executing a complex distributed transaction. To ensure consistency among all services, protocols such as two-phase commit might be used.

facts.claim: Airbnb's payments system uses write repair (every client write call attempts to repair an inconsistent, broken state via retry), which requires idempotency so that repeated identical requests move money at most once
facts.quote: Our solution in this particular post utilizes write repair, where every write call from the client to the server attempts to repair an inconsistent, broken state... it is critical a payments request gets processed completely exactly once... the underlying system should move money at most once.

facts.claim: Airbnb rejected building idempotency as a separate stand-alone service because it needed ultra-low latency and a separate service would suffer the same reliability problems it was meant to solve; it instead built Orpheus as a library so product developers would not need to specialize in data-integrity concerns
facts.quote: We needed ultra low latency, so building a separate, stand-alone idempotency service wouldn't be sufficient. Most importantly, the service would suffer from the same problems it was originally intended to solve... it would be highly inefficient to have every developer specialize on data integrity.

facts.claim: Orpheus splits every API request into three phases -- Pre-RPC (record request details in the database), RPC (make the live call to the external/downstream service), and Post-RPC (record the response, including whether an error is retryable) -- and enforces two rules: no service calls over the network during Pre/Post-RPC, and no database interaction during the RPC phase itself
facts.quote: Orpheus is centered around the assumption that almost every standard API request can be separated into three distinct phases: Pre-RPC, RPC, and Post-RPC... No service interaction over networks in Pre and Post-RPC phases. No database interactions in the RPC phases.

facts.claim: The Pre-RPC and Post-RPC database writes are each wrapped in their own single atomic database transaction using Java lambdas, so each phase either fully succeeds or fully fails, keeping network communication strictly separate from database transactions
facts.quote: every database commit in each of the Pre-RPC and Post-RPC phases is combined into a single database transaction. This ensures atomicity... all network communication, the RPC, are explicitly separated from all database transactions.

facts.claim: Exceptions are classified as retryable (5XX-style transient infrastructure/network errors, expected to eventually succeed on retry) or non-retryable (4XX-style validation/state errors such as refunding an already-refunded payment, expected to fail identically on every retry)
facts.quote: unexpected runtime exceptions due to network and infrastructure issues (5XX HTTP statuses) are retryable... We categorize validation errors, such as invalid input and states (for example, you can't refund a refund), as non-retryable (4XX HTTP statuses).

facts.claim: Clients choose between request-level idempotency (a random UUID key per logical request, e.g. to allow multiple distinct partial payments on one reservation) and entity-level idempotency (a deterministic key derived from the entity, e.g. "payment-1234-refund", so that repeated logically-equivalent requests collapse to one)
facts.quote: a random and unique key should be chosen from the client in order to ensure idempotency... An example format would be “payment-1234-refund”. Every refund request for a unique payment would consequently be idempotent at the entity-level.

facts.claim: Each request acquires a database row-level lock on its idempotency key, granting a time-bounded lease; a retry is only permitted to proceed once the current lease has expired, and Orpheus additionally enforces a maximum retryable window as a safety net against rogue retries
facts.quote: API calls, with the help of the framework, each need to acquire a database row-level lock on an idempotency key. This grants a lease... an API request can be retryable only after the current lease has expired... Orpheus additionally offers a maximum retryable window.

facts.claim: Idempotency information is always read from and written to the master database rather than a replica, because replica lag could otherwise cause a retried request to find no prior response on a lagging replica and re-execute the payment, producing a duplicate charge; the idempotency-key tables are sharded on the idempotency key itself, chosen for its high cardinality and even distribution
facts.quote: in the event of replica lag, the client could correctly fire an idempotent retry to the service and the response would not be recorded to the replica yet... the service could mistakenly execute the payment again, resulting in duplicate payments... We alleviated this by sharding the database by idempotency key.

facts.claim: Since the launch of the Orpheus framework, Airbnb achieved five nines (99.999%) of consistency for its payments while annual payment volume simultaneously doubled
facts.quote: where has Orpheus gotten Airbnb Payments so far? Since the launch of the framework, we have achieved five nines in consistency for our payments, while our annual payment volume has simultaneously doubled.

conflicts: Chew & Khisti (S70) explicitly reject Stripe's approach (S28) of a client-supplied Idempotency-Key header cached at the API edge in favor of an internal per-service library (Orpheus) that manages idempotency keys and phase-separated database transactions inside each service; both converge on the same three-state (absent/in-flight/complete) idempotency model but place the enforcement point at different layers of the stack.

sources.title: Rebuilding Payment Orchestration at Airbnb
sources.authors: Bryon Ross, Feifeng Yang, Sophie Behr, Theresa Johnson, Xin Lin, Yun Jin Cho
sources.authority: Airbnb's own account of redesigning its payment orchestration system as part of the SOA migration, connecting the Orpheus idempotency framework (S70) directly to the monolith-to-SOA transition (S31) and reporting the same five-nines consistency result years into production.

facts.claim: Airbnb's original payment models were tightly coupled to the concept of a reservation for a stay, so every new product (e.g. Experiences) required rebuilding payment-related features with product-specific quirks; the SOA migration was used as an opportunity to redesign payments around a product-agnostic data model instead of a one-to-one lift of the monolith
facts.quote: Airbnb's billing data, payment APIs, payment orchestration, and user experiences were tightly coupled with the concept of a reservation for a stay... the payments organization instead decided to use it as an opportunity to fundamentally redesign our services.

facts.claim: The redesigned payment orchestration system divides every major workflow into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of retryable idempotent steps built on the Orpheus framework, which lets the orchestration layer stay eventually consistent with the payment-gateway and product-fulfillment services and has produced five nines (99.999%) of payment consistency
facts.quote: Every major workflow is divided into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of retryable idempotent steps, each with well-defined behavior... This approach has led to five 9s (99.999%) of consistency for payments.

facts.claim: For asynchronous inter-service communication, payment services publish events over a Kafka-based message bus, and event processors apply the idempotency framework to upgrade Kafka's at-least-once delivery guarantee into an effectively-exactly-once one
facts.quote: payments services primarily use a Kafka-based message bus to send “events” to one another, and event processors use the idempotency framework to enhance the at-least-once guarantee of Kafka into an exactly-once guarantee.

facts.claim: The payments SOA migration was split into four major phases -- Pricing, Payouts, Bookings, and Data Migration -- rather than small independent functional blocks, because the team chose to redesign the underlying data model instead of doing a one-to-one port; the Bookings phase alone was further subdivided into more than 30 milestones
facts.quote: the migration for the payments systems was broken down into four major phases: Pricing, Payouts, Bookings, and Data Migration... The migration of bookings for stays was subdivided into over 30 milestones.

facts.claim: Because historical bookings were not migrated up front, Airbnb ran the legacy monolithic payment system and the new SOA payment system in parallel for most of the migration, requiring a transformation layer that converted data from either system into one unified model for client services
facts.quote: existing bookings would continue to proceed through their lifecycle in the legacy monolithic system... engineering teams needed to maintain two parallel payment orchestration systems throughout virtually the entire migration process... a new transformation layer was built to transparently retrieve data from the correct underlying source.

disagreements.topic: Strong, synchronously-replicated consistency vs. eventual consistency for large-scale storage

positions.claim: Two-phase commit over Paxos groups, with a globally synchronized clock (TrueTime), is worth its latency cost because it gives externally-consistent transactions at global scale; Spanner was built specifically because Bigtable's eventual cross-datacenter replication and lack of cross-row transactions caused frequent complaints from application teams.

For always-on, latency-critical services, ACID and cross-datacenter strong consistency are the wrong trade: Dynamo deliberately gives up consistency during failures/partitions to remain 'always writeable', pushing conflict resolution to reads and the application, because Amazon's experience showed ACID data stores 'tend to have poor availability.'

disagreements.topic: Is Raft's understandability advantage over Paxos decisive in practice?

positions.claim: Raft's decomposition (leader election / log replication / safety) is easier to teach and implement correctly: a 43-student study found participants answered Raft questions better than Paxos questions after learning both.

Production-critical systems that predate or coexist with Raft's adoption still run mature Paxos implementations rather than migrating: Chubby (behind Bigtable) and Spanner's spanservers both use Paxos, suggesting operational maturity of an existing implementation outweighs a pedagogical understandability advantage once a system is already built and hardened.
Fixed windows are simpler and cheaper to implement (a counter that resets on a clock boundary), but allow up to 2x the nominal limit in a burst that straddles a window boundary.
Sliding windows evaluate the trailing interval continuously and correctly reject the same boundary-straddling burst, at the cost of tracking request timestamps rather than a single counter.

disagreements.topic: How should token-based LLM rate limits be enforced when true cost is only known after generation?

positions.claim: Estimate pessimistically at request start and adjust the estimate as the request streams: Anthropic's ITPM is estimated at the beginning of a request and adjusted during it to reflect actual input tokens used, and OTPM counts only tokens actually generated in real time.

Admit optimistically and reconcile after the fact: Envoy AI Gateway checks whether processing a request would exceed the limit using current state, processes it, and only then counts the resulting token usage toward the total -- a design that can let a burst of concurrent requests each pass the pre-check before any of their usage lands.

disagreements.topic: Should cached tokens count against a customer's rate limit?

positions.claim: Cached input tokens should be excluded from the throughput limit: for most Claude models, cache_read_input_tokens do not count toward ITPM, so heavy prefix reuse (e.g. 80% cache hit rate) multiplies effective throughput headroom well beyond the nominal limit.

Cached input tokens should still count toward the platform's throughput limit: OpenAI's documentation states cached input tokens still count toward tokens-per-minute limits even though they are billed at a discounted rate.

disagreements.topic: Should safety moderation be a pre-generation blocking gate or a post-generation signal?

positions.claim: Moderation scores should be treated as policy signals for the calling application, not an automatic blocking decision; results should be reviewed before showing output to a user, and streamed moderation scores only arrive after the full output is generated.

Safety should be a continuous pipeline spanning policy design, training-time shaping of model behavior, pre-deployment evaluation gates, and real-time classifier enforcement across the full lifecycle -- not a single bolt-on filter step around generation.

disagreements.topic: Dedicated per-tenant GPU pools vs. shared pooled GPUs with per-key limits for inference multi-tenancy

positions.claim: Dedicated GPU clusters per model and customer tier eliminate noisy-neighbor variance, at the cost of lower aggregate utilization when a given tenant's traffic is bursty or idle.

Shared GPU pools behind a gateway that enforces per-virtual-key budgets and rate limits (LiteLLM's model) maximize utilization across tenants, accepting some risk of cross-tenant interference that must be bounded by the rate-limit/queueing layer instead of by physical isolation.

disagreements.topic: Synchronous vs. asynchronous trainer/rollout coupling in RL post-training infrastructure

positions.claim: Fully asynchronous, microservice-decoupled generation and training (with bounded staleness via version rejection, depth bounding, or importance-sampling correction) delivers large speedups: AReaL reports 2.77x over synchronous systems with comparable or better final performance, and PipelineRL's per-forward-pass weight swap keeps staleness near zero without ever blocking generation.

Bounded-queue, Ray-orchestrated designs (verl's 3D-HybridEngine resharding, NeMo-RL, SkyRL) keep training and rollout more tightly coupled through explicit resharding or a capacity-limited buffer, trading some of the asynchronous speedup for a simpler mental model and easier debugging of a single dataflow graph.

disagreements.topic: HPC batch scheduler vs. cloud-native orchestrator for GPU training clusters

positions.claim: A centralized scheduler with a simple heartbeat model (Slurm's slurmctld/slurmd) is the traditional HPC answer: one controller assigns jobs to nodes and arbitrates a pending-work queue, with no declarative reconciliation loop.

Cloud-native orchestrators (the Borg-to-Kubernetes lineage, and Ray's actor/task model) favor declarative desired-state reconciliation and finer-grained resource primitives (priority, quota, admission control in Borg; tasks/actors/object store in Ray), and are what modern RL frameworks (8 of 16 surveyed) build their trainer/rollout orchestration on top of instead of Slurm.
